items.summary: Editorial arguing that, despite the men's cross-country demotion and financial worries, the winter brought much good news, and explaining the committee's plan to set up new sub-committees to run the club.
items.text:
Many members have said that this winter's results have been a disaster, with demotion from Division One of the Surrey Cross Country League such a contrast to the track and field successes of last summer. Certainly our Cross Country Secretary Colin Pearson has been pretty fed up with the lack of support from team members over the ``country''. This, together with our Treasurer's warnings about the state of finances within the club and lack of any of the sponsorship deals enjoyed by other clubs have made it seem like a very dismal winter.

But is this really the case? One of the benefits of editing the club magazine is the gathering of news from all areas of the club and there is no doubt that, on the whole, there is far more good news to report in this edition than bad.

Our Ladies, with their wonderful team spirit, have done well to gain promotion to Division One of the Surrey League in such a positive manner, and Belgrave's young stars in the Youths and Boys team convincingly won their section of the Surrey League with the Colts also doing well to finish third. We haven't had successes like that from our youngsters since the days of Gladwin and Co. Even in the Men's Cross Country we have a new star in Kaesse Tadesse who warmed the hearts of many on a freezing day at Parliament Hill with his second place in the Junior race.

There has been a feeling on the committee for a while that some aspects of the management of the Club might need to be reviewed. Athletics has changed so much over the last ten or twenty years with the introduction of open Athletics and sponsorship and it is important that Belgrave should reflect those changes. It is also important for the club to review areas which are not doing so well and become pro-active in helping those areas.

At an extra committee meeting held specially to discuss this topic on March 1st it was decided to set up a number of sub-committees whose areas of responsibility are to cut right across the traditional sections of the Club. For instance, it is intended that the Track and Field group should cover both genders, all age groups and include track walking; the Road Running, Cross Country and Road Walking sub-committee would have a similar structure. Sub-committees are also being created for Finance, Social Activities, Sponsorship and Public Relations, Membership Services, Belgrave Hall, Relationships with external bodies and, finally, Planning and Development. The idea is that each of these groups' activities will still need to be ratified by the General Committee which, it has been suggested, should be restructured along slimmer lines than at present.

The Planning and Development sub-committee would be a sort of ``think tank'' for the club. It has already played a great role in developing and presenting the ideas of Club members who felt that it was time for our administration and organisation to be looked at critically. Some of the ideas that have come up have, to say the very least, been radical. Some, even if accepted by the current General Committee, would require changes to be made at the Annual General Meeting.

There have already been those who have said that we tried to form sub-committees before and it didn't work, while some older members have commented that the ideas are nothing new, the club used to be run this way in the past. Well, no good ideas are truly original, so hopefully Belgrave can learn from the past, make changes where they will benefit our Club and look forward to continued progress into the next century.

Help!

We are desperately in need of help!

At Southern T&F League away meetings we are supposed to provide a track judge, a timekeeper, and a team of judges for a field event. The trouble is that our two men's SL teams have eleven away matches between them this summer and so far we have no judges or timekeepers whatsoever for these meetings. Please, we have got to do something about this predicament. Couldn't you lend a hand - even just for one match? Perhaps you are a normally active athlete but currently on the injured list. It doesn't matter if you have no experience, it's willing hands that we need. items.heading: From "THE BELGRAVIAN"
items.summary: Look-back column reprinting news of members in the services from May 1943 and cross-country and road-relay reports from June 1968.
items.text:
From "THE BELGRAVIAN"

50 YEARS AGO ..... May 1943

News from members in the services:-

Lieutenant F.W. 'Billy' Pritchard of the anti-tank regiment has been killed in action in North Africa. He will be remembered as a sprinter of merit.

Captain Tommy Green recently met with a bombing accident and suffered three slight wounds.

Wally Ives, out in India, writes ``Always I am waiting for the call which means HOME and WIMBLEDON''. His letter took eleven weeks to arrive.

Arthur Beaumont says he is now in Tripoli for a rest after the big advance. Tells unusual tales about the Arabs and tent life.

Percy Wright, in South Wales, acknowledging 'The Belgravian', says ``It's equal to a flash of cockney in the heart of this place and believe me that's saying something. When the mag arrives it carries me back to stale sinks and an overcrowded bath tub''.

Alf Orton says that after 8 1/2 months in the desert he can now get in to Cairo. Hasn't felt like training; though a 2:06 time for 800 metres has nearly made him change his mind.

Flying Officer Bill Lucas found time to look in at Belgrave Hall when on leave from instructional flying duties.

Joe Flower, writing from West Africa, says of 'The Belgravian' ``What pleasure that little journal brings''.

Dan Patience, after having been stationed in the wilds of Ayr, bemoaning his fate because he couldn't get a run, now writes from North Africa! Says that all he does is marching, bathing and eating oranges.

Len Fletcher says that if he asks for leave for walking ``The beaks of this Fred Karno outfit think you want to take a WAAF out''.

Flight Sergeant Colin Sutton has hopped from the Middle East to India. He has started training again and met the Indian Champion, Simba, over 1500 metres but was beaten. There will be a return match.

Reg Shepherd, back from Canada with his ``wings'' is now in Scotland. (News has just been received that Reg has been posted missing after a reconaissance over Europe).

Knut Moe our Norwegian member, according to rumour from a neutral source, has escaped to England.

Les Bennett is still amongst the missing in Malaya. His wife Olive writes ``It is over a year since I last heard from my husband. I have not given up hope and have great confidence that he is safe and well''.

25 YEARS AGO ..... JUNE 1968

Cross-Country

``Many of our members will consider that 4th place in the ``National'' at Sutton Coldfield was a good performance but to those of us who know the potential of our runners this was a most disappointing result. This is the THIRD year in succession that we have occupied 4th position and although we move nearer and nearer to the leaders year by year there is no doubt that this year's team could have won handsomely given the right preparation and right approach. Tony Fairclough was unlucky to suffer two bad falls. 11th Gerry North, 31st Geoff North, 45th John Thresher, 78th Adrian Major, 87th Bill Dance, 102nd Peter Whewell, 139th Laurie O'Hara, 160th Trevor Hart, 179th Tony Fairclough.''

Road Relays

``Two firsts, two seconds and two thirds. Our best for many years. That must be the undisputed verdict on a spring road-relay season that saw our team do battle on six occasions and return home with awards every time. The peak of this brief but high powered season was undoubtedly the National 12-stage Relay at Leicester where Coventry Godiva, aided and abetted by our ``own'' Mel Thorpe, ran out deserved winners. That Derby should edge us out of the silver by just 11 seconds may seem rough justice. Including our reserve (Dabbs) five of our thirteen runners are over 30 years of age, headed by Bill Kerr, 36. The average age of the team is 28yrs 4mths. It will be up to our three under-24's Bicourt, Major and Donnison to share an ever increasing degree of responsibility in our future teams, especially with the loss of Peter Whewell to South Africa, Gerry Williams to Venezuela, Chris Steer to Canada and Geoff North to retirement (again).

Thanks for your help

There was a great response to my request for your assistance in helping me complete my sets of athletics magazines. Thanks to the following people I am now only 8 issues short of every "Athletics Weekly" going back to when it actually became a weekly in 1950:

John and Pam Davies, Leo Coy, Pete Mulholland (Hercules Wimbledon AC), Colin Pearson, Tom Morell, Tommy Thomas (South London H), Charlie Jones, Arthur Penstone, Win Shepherd, Nina Mills, Bob Bridges, Charlie Dickinson and Martin Duff (Aldershot F&D).

Nina dug out some copies of "Women's Athletics" which make for some interesting reading. This was a short-lived sister magazine to "AW" lasting just twelve issues from May '68 to April '69. It contains some gems like,

"... following a beauty routine both during the week and on the day of competition ..."

and featured a male track pin-up each month! Maybe "The Belgravian" could pick up a few tips here.

Arthur Penstone came up with a nice little run of "The Belgravian" from the early '30s and Tom Morell has passed on some copies of "Amateur Athlete", a weekly produced by Armour Milne during the War years.

items.heading: Kaessa breaks the drought
items.summary: Report on the English Cross Country Championships at Parliament Hill on 27 February, led by Kaesse Tadesse's second place in the Junior race, with Youth, Junior and Senior race accounts and results.
items.text:
Kaessa breaks the drought

ENGLISH CC CHAMPS., PARLIAMENT HILL, 27 FEB

A magnificent second place by Kaesse Tadesse in the Junior Men's race warmed the hearts of Belgrave supporters in the Arctic conditions of Parliament Hill fields. We have had a long, barren stretch as far as cross country goes. There have been relatively successful Belgrave Junior teams, and our Juniors and Seniors were near the front in the early to mid-sixties but how long is it since a Belgravian last took home a ``National'' cross country medal of any variety?

Charlie Dickinson and Alan Mead report

Returning to the famous course for the first time since Julian Goater won by nearly two minutes in 1981, and although the strength of the fields was perhaps weakened by the revamped Inter-Counties/ International Trial three weeks before, the National nevertheless produced three very exciting races. The course had been slightly altered because of gas maintenance work around Kenwood and therefore had even more twists, turns and undulations than in previous years. This together with numerous boggy patches left by the winter rain, the terrible uphill start, and a freezing wind bringing squalls of snow from the north, certainly produced a test of the ``traditional'' kind.

Youth 7k

The youngest age group was the one that promised most for Belgrave in the way of team positions. Our lads could mostly be classed as belonging to the shorter middle-distance group, perhaps not best suited to 7,000 metres over Parliament Hill. However, it was felt that a team place inside the top ten might just be on the cards.

Imagine the excitement then, when after the charge up the starting hill, Ben Hamill was placed handily on the shoulder of joint favourite Scott West, leading the field as they went over the top. As if that wasn't enough the cheeky blighter had the audacity to wink to the Belgrave supporters cheering him on. Unfortunately even bold Ben couldn't sustain this sort of action for the full distance. The loss of a shoe together with his extravagant start had him spinning back through the field to a position well below his potential.

Adam Jones was another who would have expected to place a lot higher, so in spite of a brilliant 34th from Matt Hillier, who was really flying over the last section of the race, and an equally impressive 54th from Gavin Mason, the team had to settle for 17th. Nevertheless, we were still 4th Southern team home.

1, K.Farrow (Derby & C) 21:15; 2, W.Levett (Tonbridge) 21:35; 3, B.Noad (Bristol) 21:47; ... 34, M.Hillier 22:48; 54, G.Mason 23:09; 180, M.Anderson 24:48; 232, B.Hamill 25:36; 240, A.Jones 25:41; 335, T.Earle 30:39.
Teams: 1, Derby & C 68; 2, Oxford City 155; 3, Royal Sutton Coldfield 181; ... 17, Belgrave 500; 39 teams closed in.

Junior 10k

In the Junior race, Kaesse was well to the front of a large leading group at the start, then began to force the pace in the long downhill sweep coming out of the South Meadow on the first lap. This broke the field, apart from Spencer Barden who had won so convincingly in the South of Thames a month before, Tim Dickinson, running a 'blinder' for Blackheath, and Stefan White of Coventry Godiva, runner up at Luton in 1991, and running for the third time as a Junior.

These four continued to battle it out as the race entered the second lap with Barden, the favourite, now leading and Kaesse clinging to third place. But this effort visibly tired the strong looking GEC Avionics man, giving Stefan White his chance. With Kaesse hanging on like grim death, White made his move half way through the final lap and the pair quickly opened up a huge gap over Barden.

As they swept around Kite hill to the finish, Kaesse made one final spirited effort to close a five yard gap, but White's strength and experience prevailed and he pulled away round the fields to the finish.

For a man who dislikes the cold, dislikes the mud, and dislikes hills, Kaesse had run so very well.

Danny Winson was our only other Junior. For a man who competes over 400 and 800 metres in our track teams, Danny has been showing good form in his last few cross country races but he too suffered from a shoe lost to the glutinous Hampstead mud.

Interestingly, only four of the twenty-six teams that finished had a full complement of six runners.

1, S.White (Coventry Godiva 29:42; 2, K.Tadesse (Belgrave) 29:49; 3, S.Barden (GEC Avionics) 30:14; ... 161, D.Winson 35:27.

Senior 15k

The Seniors were led home by Jim Estall who ran what appeared to be a comfortable race. Owain Lewes was next scorer and ran probably his best race of the season. He ran in bare feet which seemed ideal for the conditions but strange for someone who sells running shoes. Perhaps he knows more than we do! Mike Lake ran another steady race.

items.heading: Dougie gets it wrong - and wins !
items.summary: Result of the previous issue's photo competition (the picture was of Leo Coy, prize to Doug Maughan) and a new teaser asking readers to name the faces in a crowd photo of Belgrave supporters taken at a South Coast resort.
items.text:
Dougie gets it wrong - and wins !

We weren't exactly inundated with entries for the competition set in the last issue. Who was that smart young fellow depicted on page 49? Well, two people had a crack:

Bert Stroud reckoned it was a young Don Anderson, thinking about slipping out to go train-spotting. Doug Maughan, on the other hand, thought it was Jim Heathfield. ``I've had my picture taken, read the lesson, what next? I thought I was joining a running club!'' (Incidentally, Doug thinks that Jim looks just as smart in 1993, even in his long trousers.

Sorry lads, you're both wrong. The photo' was of Leo Coy and we reckon it was a shot of him learning his lines for reading out the season's best performances at the 1952 Club Dinner!

Anyway, we had a prize lined up, and it was Doug's name that came out of the hat. He is now the proud owner of a copy of the Track Statistician's Bible - The ATFS Athletics 1992 Handbook. See, it was worth entering.

Have a go at this issue's teaser. A prize will be awarded to the person who can put the most names to faces in the accompanying photograph below. As a tie-breaker you'd better tell us a bit about the occasion as well! We'll give you a clue - the picture was taken at a well known South Coast resort.

items.heading: Membership moans
items.summary: Carl Lawton complains that over 80 members had not paid their subscriptions by 23 March, some of them well-known athletes, and sarcastically suggests making subscriptions optional.
items.text:
Membership moans

I am sure all club members will be pleased to be aware of the Club's financial problems and the efforts some of their elected officials go to, to ensure the careful management of our limited resources. We are not a sponsored Club and have to rely on subscription and generous donations from members. Unfortunately we are blighted, as no doubt other organisations are, by a proportion of ``members'' who decline to pay these subs. As at March 23rd over 80 ``names'' are outstanding. Regretably some of these are well known and, in cases, from their gains from the many major athletic meetings at which they compete, it is unfortunate that they cannot see their way to providing the Club with the small amount that is requested.

For those of you that would criticise that some of these are poor and live a hand to mouth existence, well, this may be the case, but we can only help if we are informed. Non-reply to letters tells us nothing.

One simple way out of this annual predicament is to make subscriptions optional: only send out one reminder per year and let the Club stew from lack of finance. This will make my job nice and easy and then I won't have an axe to grind about non-payers.

Carl Lawton

items.heading: Sidetracks
items.summary: Club gossip column with news of members old and new: reminiscences of trips to the 1936 Berlin and 1960 Rome Olympics, injuries to Paul King, Gary Staines and Lewis Samuel, a Merton civic reception for the European Clubs' team, and Julia Cockram's return to high jumping.
items.text:
Sidetracks

Tony Whatley, an old friend of Tony Verdie's from some way back, turned out for the Belgrave Half-Marathon, hoping to renew their acquaintanceship. He sends his regards and hopes to catch up with him soon at some other race.

Colin Pearson bumped into Alf Horton a few months back. Alf is well and asks that his best wishes be passed on to all that remember him up at the Hall.

We read in the Veterans Athletic Club Newsletter that Cecil Gittins has been elected President of that Club for 1992-93. The newsletter goes on to praise him as one of the hardest working officials in our sport, something that we in Belgrave can only endorse. Congratulations, Cecil.

Good old Marcello! Together with his willing band of helpers, his hard work in organising another Sunday afternoon Italian ``binge'' at the Hall netted the Club nigh on £200.

Tom Carter has been corresponding with one of his old colleagues Dave Main, who is now living in Tournon in France where he is converting a barn to a small house. Previously he had lived in Karpathos, Greece for seven years. Dave recalls the lads of '46.
``Oh! What happy days they were. I can still re-live our training runs around the Common and sometimes into Richmond Park, you pushing as all to the limit (except for the odd day when you were not feeling so good) and then Len Herbert or myself would try and push you - great fun it was. It does not seem to have done the members any harm either, they all seem to be steaming past the eighties and into the nineties - long may they go on.''
Dave keeps fit by hitting the odd golf ball. One of his sons has run the Boston and London Marathons and he has a nephew who has also completed the ``London''.

Hearing about the prospective trip by a Belgrave party to Stuttgart for the World Championships, Charlie Jones recalls the trip he made with fellow Belgravians to the Berlin Olympics in 1936. He had to save for two and a half years to rake together the £35 they each needed for the jaunt. Charlie remembers the rail and boat fare figure to this day - five pounds, nine shillings and seven pence halfpenny! They combined the athletics with a walking holiday along the Rhine, staying at Youth Hostels.
Charlie had a fall just a year ago and doesn't get out as regularly as he used to but both he and Betty are well.

Win Shepherd too recalls a Belgrave trip on the Continent - to the Rome Olympics of 1960. They had trouble from the start when they couldn't get into their hotel room due to its occupancy by a group of Polish swimmers who were refusing to leave as one of their number had got to the finals. They managed to get put up elsewhere and Harry Shields ended up in the hotel Manager's flat - immaculate decorations including a marble floor - and the first thing he did was set up a primus stove on the floor to brew up a cup of tea.

We understand that Sheena Lucas underwent a hip replacement operation a few months ago but has been making a good recovery. Our best wishes go to her and we look forward to seeing her at one or other of our summer competitions.

A fractured limb has been the lot of walker Paul King this winter. Motorcyclist Paul now shares a little more in common with Barry Sheene, having had an assortment of steel pins inserted in his leg to hold it together after a collision with a car. Actually Paul was lucky he didn't get his other leg broken as well, for when Messrs. Warburton and Lawton arranged to go and see him in hospital, they only found out by chance that he had discharged himself without telling anyone. Believe it or not it wasn't too long before 'Kingy' was managing to get up to the Hall again on training nights - and even if he couldn't get out for a spin, he took advantage of the Club showers. But amazingly, as we go to print, we find that not only is Paul out training again but is planning to enter one of the Veterans Walks at Battersea in a few days!

Unfortunately a little more news about those on the injured list. Poor Gary Staines is, if nothing else, learning how to be patient. Having completed the long haul back to fitness after his achilles tendon problems and operation and with the track season all but upon him, he has now suffered troubles with a calf muscle and at best is likely to have to put his season back a bit.

But for 400 metre star Lewis Samuel the season is already over due to a ruptured achilles tendon, perhaps the worst of athletic injuries and one which hit him, we believe, while playing basketball in Lanzarote. To Lewis and all others on the injured list we send our hopes for a speedy recovery and return to the team.

An interesting document to come the way of ``The Belgravian'' Editorial Offices is a copy of a completed application for a US National Collegiate Championships record. Mike Edwards, representing his Texas outfit Abiline Christian University, vaulted 5.25m to help his team win the competition at the Dakotadome, Vermilion, on March 13th.

A dozen or so members of our track and field team gathered in the Mayor of Merton's Parlour on the evening of Monday 5th April. The Mayor had been thrilled to find out that Great Britain was being represented in the European Clubs' Championship by a team from his own borough and wanted to be introduced to the Bels. He presented a Merton Borough flag for us to fly in Budapest and the Council made a most generous donation towards the costs of transporting the team to Hungary.

Haringey's Dalton Grant is a fine ambassador for our sport and we have him to thank - although he probably doesn't know it - for the re-launching of the athletic career of Julia Cockram.
Julia's 1.59m High Jump, set as an Under-13 in May 1980, has stood the test of time and still ranks as the equal 9th best performance ever by a British Minor Girl. Third on that list is current international Debora Marti's 1.65m, also from 1980. As a 15 year old Julie competed for Surrey in the English Schools Championships, clearing 1.75m, but like many others it was not long before she dropped out of the sport. Luckily, however, that was not the end of the story.
A chance meeting with Dalton and the exchange of a few enthusiastic words about the jumping that she used to do when she was a schoolgirl was all that was required to make her think about getting fit again. And looking for a club, she fortunately decided upon Belgrave. Good old Dalton!

items.heading: OBITUARY F.A. "Mickey" Walker (1908-1992)
items.summary: Obituary of F.A. 'Mickey' Walker (1908-1992), a supporting cross-country runner of the 1930s and 1940s who won the Surrey County 20-mile title and later lived in Cornwall.
items.text:
OBITUARY
F.A. ``Mickey'' Walker
(1908-1992)

Mickey Walker was a contemporary of Tom Carter's. Both were born in 1908; they joined Belgrave within nine months of each other and later in their lives went into business together.

He was not one of the stars who featured in our formidable teams of the '30s and '40s, but he was a sound supporting runner who frequently featured in 12-to-score teams and on one occasion was just pipped for sixth scorer by Alf Taylor when the ``Southern'' was held at Taplow.

In the late 1930s he concentrated on distance running with some success. He gained a 1st Class standard in the Polytechnic Marathon of 1938 and the following year won the Surrey County '20' title ahead of the legendary Bert Footer who was making his debut at the distance.

His success in this race led to an over-confident start in the Polytechnic Marathon where ``he blazed through the first five miles in sub-28 minutes'' (Belgravian) - quite a pace in those days. He faded to a creditable 12th. Seeing Footer finish 3rd made him wonder what might have been.

Unlike Carter, Walker did not regard Belgrave as a major part of his life and when he moved to Cornwall he allowed his membership to lapse. He re-joined the Club in 1963, at Tom's instigation, and visited Belgrave Hall very occasionally. He died at his Cornwall home in 1992 at the age of 84 years. Our commiserations are extended to his family and friends.

Clive Shippen

items.text:
Indoor Track & Field

BIRMINGHAM GAMES, NIA, 8/9 JAN

Fred Salle had a clear margin over Cannock & Stafford's Barrington Williams and sharpened up with a bit of speedwork in the 60m as well. The sprints were dominated by young pretenders but Phil Goedluck showed he was in good shape, reaching the final and ending up only 1/10th off his best outdoor time for last season.

60m: (heats) P.Goedluck 6.94; F.Salle 7.10. 200m: 5, P.Goedluck 21.59; (semis) J.Ridgeon 22.08. 3000m: 15, R.Turner 8:30.90. 60mH: 7, N.Owen 8.17. HJ: 6, A.Hutchinson 2.00. LJ: 1, F.Salle 7.60. PV: 6, D.McDermott 4.60. SP: 3, L.Marar 15.75.

PEARL INTERNATIONAL GAMES, KELVIN HALL, GLASGOW, 30 JAN

Fred Salle had the indoor jump of a lifetime when in the first round he cut the sand at 7.96 metres for a Club Record, only 9cm behind the UK best and just 1cm shy of his outdoor pb set in 1986. He followed up with a no jump but still held the lead going into the 3rd round when World Record holder Mike Powell managed to register a lacklustre (for him) 8.07. Powell went on to record an all-comers record of 8.36 with his last leap. Fred also got in a 7.82 to back up but slipped to 4th as Russians Bogrianov and Tarasenko crept past him.

Paul Edward's series in the shot read 18.17, 18.20, x, 17.86, 17.82, x, but he too suffered at the hands of two Russians; Nikolayev and Smirnov reached 20.38 and 19.83.

VAUXHALL INTERNATIONAL, NIA, BIRMINGHAM 13 FEB

The GB versus USA indoor match always generates a lot of excitement on this side of the Atlantic but unfortunately rather less in the hearts of the away team. Once again the American outfit was devoid of many of the top names in T&F and they suffered a resounding defeat as a result.

Marcus Adam and John Regis returned from off-season training in sunny California to don British singlets and lined up together in the one lap race against the rising young Briton Darren Campbell. The two Belgravians had no trouble in putting him and the Americans down with John just shading Marcus as they crossed the line. Unfortunately the former had clearly taken a shorter than legal route to the line and was disqualified. These three later teamed up with Windsor's Mark Richardson to defeat the USA team in the 4x200 relay, 1:23.56 to 1:23.79.

As usual Paul Edwards had far too much muscle for his domestic opposition but was in turn well beaten by the three Americans with Olympic Champion Stulce setting an all-comers record of 21.77. Fred Salle continued his solid indoor season and had every right to be pleased with his 2nd place, but the winner only recorded 7.76 and a repeat of his Glasgow form would have given him victory.

200m: 1, M.Adam 21.06; J.Regis dsq unofficial time 21.0. LJ: 2, F.Salle 7.51. SP: 4, P.Edwards 18.56.

TSB INTERNATIONAL, NIA, BIRMINGHAM, 20 FEB

Neither John Regis or Marcus Adam had the World Indoor Championships pencilled into their programmes but their performances at the NIA showed that they would most certainly have been medal contenders. Marcus was edged in the final straight by Bulgaria's Antonov as they set the 3rd and 4th fastest times in the World this winter, 20.84 and 20.89. (A Russian was to go a fraction faster in Bercy on the same afternoon and an American performed similarly next day in Boston.) But John was not to be outdone. At the 200m point in his 300m race he was hand-timed at 20.9 and went on to win as he pleased in 32.98 - 8/100ths behind the British best.

TSB AAA INDOOR CHAMPS., NIA, BIRMINGHAM, 27 FEB

The Shot competition gave the Bels their only ``gold'', courtesy of Paul Edwards of course, but it is really worth taking note of Leith Marar's performances this winter. His best outdoor mark of 15.40 dates from 1990 and is surely due for revision. In indoor meeting after meeting he has peppered the 15.50 area - might we see a 16m plus effort when summer comes around? Warren Caswell had the pleasure of sharing 3rd place in the high jump with Geoff Parsons, and Phil Goedluck put two fine runs together in the one lap race, 21.64 to win heat 3 by five metres and then 21.62 for 5th in the final.

60m: ht. 6, L.Campbell 7.26. 200m: 5, P.Goedluck 21.62. 60mH: ht. 5, R.Hunter 8.40; 3, N.Owen 7.99. HJ: =3, W.Caswell 2.15. SP: 1, P.Edwards 18.47; 9, L.Marar 15.57.

WORLD INDOOR CHAMPS., TORONTO, 12-14 MAR

Fred Salle had every reason to be pleased with his indoor season, culminating in his selection for this fourth edition of the World Championships. A reproduction of his Kelvin Hall form should have seen him in the final and another few centimetres on top might even have put a medal within his grasp. But sometimes luck just runs the wrong way. Two ``no jumps'' left him with one last attempt to force his way into the final and how galling it was to find that red flag going up yet again for a marginal violation of the plasticene. No distance recorded for Fred while the 'bronze' went at 7.98 with Fred's best of the season 7.96!

Better luck had come Belgrave's way on day one when Shot Putter Paul Edwards was in action. Nineteen-sixty was required to guarantee progression to the final but only four athletes could reach that and Paul's second round effort of 18.23 saw him comfortably into the last twelve. The USA's Stulce had led the way in the qualifier and although fellow American Doehring led for four rounds, Stulce did the business again with a 5th putt of 21.27. Paul, meantime, confirmed his rating of 9th at these games with a 3rd round 18.32.

items.heading: Hunter aims for 7,000 points
items.summary: Decathlete Richard Hunter, a West London Institute student, describes his background as a hurdler, his injuries and finances, and his aim to score 7,000 points, with his training week, decathlon scores and 110m hurdles progression.
items.text:
Hunter aims for 7,000 points

In September 1992 multi-eventer Richard Hunter upped his decathlon pb beyond the 6,000 mark for the first time. We invited Richard, a student at the West London Institute to tell us about himself and his aims for the future.

I came to London, Isleworth in 1990 to study at W.L.I.H.E. where I am presently in my final year of a sports science degree. Having moved to the area from the North East I wanted to join a good ``local'' club. At the time I was only doing 110 metre hurdles and saw Belgrave as the ideal choice in terms of getting the races when I needed them. Unfortunately I have been hindered by injuries since coming to London.

As a 110 metre hurdler I competed for my old club Gateshead Harriers and was second in two English Schools finals, 1987 and 1989. I also gained a GB Junior international vest in 1989. While I was still a Junior in 1990, I won the AAA 60 metres hurdles indoor title, but was again hampered by injuries in the summer season of that year. I then spent 1991 hurdling and messed about in two decathlons to get an idea of what I could do. In the winter of 1991 I decided to train for the multi-events, without having a coach to help me.

I guess my favourite events are the 110 metre hurdles, long jump, 400 metres, but I actually enjoy them all. The only event that frustrates me is the javelin, for obvious reasons. In terms of aims, I have many long term and short term goals some of which include first of all breaking 6,500 points and 7,000 points. Then from there I would like to keep improving in 1994 and beyond.

Athletics is a vital part of my life and I love the training as much as the competitions but the last two to three years have been hard, with injuries, lack of a coach (until Greg Richards came along), living off a student grant, and change of environment from the North East, where facilities are so good and free, with great people to train with and motivate you, to London where the tracks take so long to get to (eg. Haringey sessions involve three hours travelling time) and sometimes cost far too much! Then at the moment I have got to get orthotics for my shoes, which are going to cost me £170! On top of this I made sure I could go warm weather training in 1991 and 1992, both out of my own funds. This year my coach has gone with the group to Cyprus again but I was not able to go due to financial reasons.

As far as my life outside athletics is concerned, I also have a part-time job as a gym instructor at a club in Twickenham. I also like music, clubs, movies, and travelling - there's always something to do.

items.heading: WALKING TO SUCCESS
items.summary: Paul Warburton invites members to try racewalking at Tuesday evening 2.7k races in Battersea Park, arguing walkers have better chances of representative honours, with the summer race dates.
items.text:
WALKING TO SUCCESS
A chance to try something different -

From small acorns grow unexpected opportunities of athletic stardom. This summer if you're in the vicinity of Battersea Park on certain Tuesday evenings listed at the end, why not give racewalking a try?

Now just before you turn the page because you wouldn't be seen dead bum wiggling, at least give me the rest of the paragraph. What are your current chances of county, international or major championship honours?

I would reckon that if you are athletically fit and open-minded the British walker has six times greater chances of doing one of the above than the British runner. Six times? A top road running field is 300 - a top walking field is 50. Every current Belgravian walker (aged between 30 and 60) has won a representative honour of some sort. Candidly, the British walking standard is not that strong. Some international vests in recent years have been won, especially by females, with remarkable ease.

I was an average runner in 1982: 25:50 was my best for 5 miles. Giving walking a go was a means of recovering from injury. I decided to stick with it. By 1986 I had won National team medals, Southern area championships, county championships, and a sackfull of open race medals and prizes.

Kerry Saxby was part of the excellent 'Little League' system in Australia where young children have a dabble at all athletic events, and discovered her event when she had a go at walking after an average showing at running, throwing, etc. At the time of writing she has just won another major championships medal indoors at Toronto to go with the 28 world records or bests already posted by the Queensland girl.

Of course, anybody that knows anything, knows that walking is not a soft option. It's not easier than running. For a start it's the only event that combines technique and aerobic effort. And so it has cardio-vascular benefits the equal of running without the threat of accompanying injury.

I'm not saying walking is for you. But it's like eating something new. If you've never tried it, how can you say you don't like it? Why not give walking one try before rejecting it? You might discover a new athletic career ...

Paul Warburton

SURREY CC LEAGUE, DIV. 2 RACE 1, TILFORD, 24 OCT

Times are changing. In the opening match last season Jacinta Moore had to take on the other Surrey clubs single-handed and not surprisingly, as a team, we ended up in last position. This time around, however, our ladies started the season in the mood to battle for promotion back up to Division One, and on the sandy hills of the Tilford course, the toughest on which we compete, we turned out a full squad of five to score plus three more backing up. Helen Maskrey led the way and with some of our sprinters getting into the scoring positions we were pleased to finish as 2nd team, not too far behind Tadworth.

In the intermediate race over 3.5k Jessica Dash was 18th in 17:49 and Laura Wilson was 5th in the minor's event, taking 10:03 for the 2.5k.

It took Helen 16:29 to tour the testing hills of the Reigate Priory and she was just under a minute slower than the fastest time of the day for her 4th place on leg one. Nina Mills was next away, clocking 19:02 to bring the team in 9th, and a now constantly improving Jacqui Smiter enjoyed herself on the final leg, picking off two of the opposition with her 17:56 effort. With Morag Andrew and Gabby Collison drafted into the team it became a fight to get into the scoring five and the overall result was a resounding win for the Bels. and a fine individual victory for Helen.

This course might be normally classed as flat and grassy but heavy rain had turned parts of the circuit into a leg-sapping quagmire - and then there was the descent down the slippery banks and through the muddy waters of the River Hogsmill to contend with on each lap! Eventually it was the two 'Js' who filled out the score sheet, pushing Nina Mills back to become our 6th placer.

But watch out for the young woman who was next home and making her debut in Belgrave colours. Martina Ryan is no stranger to cross-country, having run regularly as a junior back in Ireland. It shouldn't take her too long to run off the few intervening years of inactivity, particularly as the Ryan family are in residence at the 'King of Denmark'; how convenient for training from Belgrave Hall just around the corner.

SURREY CC CHAMPS., COULSDON, 12 DEC

Bright sunshine prevailed for the county championships but conditions were sticky underfoot and by the end of the afternoon it was pretty cold as well. The start entailed a swift couple of circuits around the field at Fox Common before the pack headed off down into Happy Valley with Woking's Zara Hyde making the running. Helen Maskrey was in the leading bunch of half a dozen and with Gabrielle Collison and Morag Andrew shoulder to shoulder close behind and only three to score, our hopes of getting into the medals looked good.

Hyde proved to be in devastating form, getting right away from the field for a clear win, but the team race turned out to be a very close affair. Woking, of course, had a good start with the individual winner but while waiting for the rest of their squad, Croydon got two home with 4th and 6th and Herne Hill were also in the frame with 7th and 9th. Then, with Helen fighting up the final slope to spearhead our team with 11th place, chased by Woking's second scorer and Herne Hill's third, we saw Morag and Gabby appear at the top of the long drag up from the Valley in 14th and 17th places. Minds numbed from the cold found it too difficult to keep four lots of mental arithmetic going but with Croydon's last scorer still nowhere in sight we began to feel sure of bronze medals.

But it was not to be so! Croydon had to wait until 30th place to get their last girl home but their early scorers were just too far up for us to counter. Next year maybe?

After this third race in the series it was beginning to look as if the Bels. were not only going to be assured of a return to the top division next winter but would probably go up as Division Two Champions both in the team and individual events. A second win over Stragglers meant that we were now 3pts clear with first match winners Tadworth a further 3pts down. Helen was top of the individual list. INTER-COUNTIES CHAMPS., Inc. UK WORLD CC TRIALS, CORBY, 6 FEB

For someone who hadn't really done any cross country before the start of this winter, Helen Maskrey has become involved in a big way. Her running in the County Championships earned her a Surrey vest and here she was along with the cream of the nation's distance runners competing in the trial for the International Champs. The race was won by Suzanne Rigg of Cheshire in 18:38 but Helen was well into the first half of the field, placing 130th of the 305 finishers, in 21:44. What a warm up for the following day's ...

26.2/SECURICOR 10k, Inc. SURREY CHAMPS, WEST EWELL, 7 FEB

A huge field set out from Hook Arena on the 10k circuit that takes in Chessington, Malden Rushett and Epsom Common before returning to West Ewell. Some familiar faces were to be seen along the way, marking the course: Billy Bull and our Kingsmeadow gang, Leo Coy - even Sue Porter out doing some training.

Your cycle-bourne reporter found it impossible to pick out all our ladies during the initial rush but did notice Jacqui Smiter and Martina Ryan in close company. Having let the field pass, some furious pedalling was necessary to work back towards the top of the pack. As the faster runners were picked up and the field became more spread out, there was still no sign of a Belgrave vest - maybe I had missed our top three. But no, the fact was that they were startlingly way up the field and as Chessington Zoo was neared, the slim frame of Gabby Collison could be seen bobbing along with her characteristic, easy style. A few more turns of the pedals and there were Morag and Helen, stride for stride with only Moyra Jordan of Horsham up ahead. My goodness, after last year's 2nd place, we were going to "walk" the team race with packing like this!

Racing ahead to find a "photo spot", the runners were not seen again until they turned into Horton Lane with nearly 2 miles to go. It was Morag who appeared first, running fiercely with Helen some 20 metres in arrears. An International runner for Scotland a few years back, Morag has had a couple of years out of the sport during which time she has started a family but now she shows all the signs of edging back to some good class running again.

On to the finish. Jordan was first through the gates and onto the grassy finishing area but before she had crossed beneath the final banner a girl in claret and gold had also turned onto the straight. It was Helen. Somewhere along that final long road she had got ahead of her rival - but only just, because a mere three seconds separated them. Second and third, and now here was Gabby, all three of our scorers on the finish straight at the same time.

Further down the field more fine running was evident. Jacqui had smashed her pb and Martina had made a fine first appearance on the road in Belgrave colours.

Of course we did win the team race and when it came to the County Championship we had the perfect score of 6 points for 1st, 2nd and 3rd. Apparently this has never been done before in a Senior Surrey championship.

SURREY CC LEAGUE, DIV. 2 RACE 4, LLOYD PARK 13 MAR

What a contrast to the day of the men's league race in early January. Then the course had been a morass and spirits were as low as the heavy grey clouds, with the Bels. due to suffer another hammering. But come the spring and the women's race, we had a firm, dry, grassy course (albeit a little rutted), beautiful blue skies, a picnic atmosphere and the certain prospect of promotion to division one.

After the very first kilometre there were a few surprises to note. Morag Andrew had made a determined start and was clearly placed ahead of our normal team leader, Helen Maskrey. Gabby Collison was close behind and then came Martina Ryan, already away from Jacqui Smiter for the first time in the series and moving strongly. These positions were not to change throughout the duration of the surely over-length race. Helen did not seem unduly worried by playing second fiddle for a change and one got the impression that the following day's Belgrave Half-Marathon was on her mind. Poor Jacqui was struggling though, troubled by stomach cramps that made a fight with Martina impossible. But there was no doubt at all that the latter was having a brilliant race and, the possessor a good "running" brain, we can look for a lot more to come from her yet. The past few weeks had seen her ease off from the Club-night runs with the men, with a switch of emphasis to sustained, fast, shorter runs on the grass of the Common. Well done Martina!

Just outside the scoring five Jacinta Moore made a welcome return to the team. Incredible though it may seem, she had been due to give birth on just about the date of this race, but baby Cliona had conveniently seen fit to enter the world a month early, leaving Jacinta to gradually get back into her running, avoiding the cold days and taking it as it comes.

Once again young Laura Wilson flew the flag for Belgrave in the minors' event with a very strong race for 4th place.

Veterans' Results

SURREY COUNTY VETERANS CC CHAMPS., RICHMOND PARK, 17 OCT

In the middle of one of the wettest Autumns in memory, the Surrey Vets Cross Country Championships managed as usual to pick a bright, sunny afternoon, although a stiff breeze chilled the runners especially as they ran past the lake. There was a good turn out of 18 from Belgrave, including two ladies, in a field of 120 runners and there was a welcome first appearance for the "newly turned forty" Mike Gleave.

At the front the race was dominated by Thames Hare and Hounds with Dave Hill winning as he pleased and Mike Farmery, another new Vet, coming through strongly for second ahead of Chris Hughes and a tired Charlie Dickinson. Rex Bale ran well to finish in the first thirty with Alan Painter completing the scoring three.

The Belgrave fifties team were rather unfortunate not to get a medal. Tony Stone limped out of the race with a pulled a hamstring at the end of the first lap which left Tony Hardy to lead in a scoring three made up by John Wasbrough and Mike Newton. It was nice to see Mike racing for the first time since his eye operation in the summer.

The race organisers, Ranelagh, were awarding an over sixties team category for the first time and the rampant Belgrave trio of Pat Newell, Bert Stroud and Charlie Walker came away with the team gold scoring the minimum of six points. The M60 race was won by Jim Chandler of Waverley but close behind there was a right ding dong between the three Belgrave runners. Eventually a rather out of sorts Charlie Walker was dropped by the in form Bert Stroud, with Pat Newell tucked in behind. At the finish a very fit and determined Pat just got the better of Bert to take individual silver. Another triumph for our over sixties team!

CAMBRIDGE H VETERANS RELAYS, ROCHESTER, 20 DEC

The Belgrave over 50 team made their annual successful Christmas pilgrimage to Rochester for the 4x2.6m road relay around the aerodrome, although they found the opposition rather tougher this year. These relays are becoming increasingly popular, with teams from Swindon, Aldershot and Woodford Green supplementing the usual Kent based contingent. The event, organised by David Coward, is sponsored by a local butcher and there is much meat given out at the end in the way of prizes. Perhaps Belgrave were a little lucky to collect their joints of pork. We finished fourth but as the third team were Cambridge "B", the Bels. were deemed the third club to finish. It's all very friendly.

Best run of the day was again from Tony Verdie who seems to like this event. He completed the second fastest lap in 13:51 to Davidson's 13:39. Having done his usual Potteries Marathon in October, Tony finds this event far enough away from his next major marathon, usually the London, to risk testing his speed. Well Tony, the speed is obviously still there, pity we can't get you onto the track!

VETERANS AC CC CHAMPS, WIMBLEDON, 23 JAN

No less than eleven Belgravians preferred to run in the VAC Championships rather than the Club '10' held on the same day, at the same time, and over roughly the same course. The VAC Championships are always well organised, with trophies and medals in five year age groups, very competitive, with the course demanding but of a reasonable length.

The Vet in form is Bob Treadwell, a full minute ahead of Tony Simmonds in the home international at Belfast, Surrey Senior Champion at Coulsdon in December, and 23rd in the South of England. When he arrived at the start the result was a foregone conclusion. It is interesting that the quality at the "sharp end" now rivals the Southern Vets Championships. The depth has been there for some years but now VAC are beginning to pick up more members from, for example, Kent and North London.

It was Grenville Tuck who led the leading bunch over the golf course and down through the woods with Charlie Dickinson starting more cautiously in sixth place. Both came unstuck in the mud through the fields at the bottom where Treadwell began to force the pace ahead of Morten and Daniel of Blackheath. Charlie moved up to third on the horse ride and chased hard, but Treadwell moved steadily away on lap two and the very strong Hugh Morten maintained the gap for 2nd.

Treadwell broke the course record set last year by Terry Osbourne and said afterwards that without the Southern in his legs from the week before, and on firmer ground he might have been close to 24 minutes! His elder brother John, a regular and popular member of VAC, took the M45 trophy.

Nor did the wet conditions stop Maggie Statham from breaking the W35 record again or our own Laurie O'Hara from bringing the M60 record down to an amazing 28:16. The quality of the M60's was such that Bert Stroud, Charlie Walker and Pat Newell all missed medals in spite of excellent runs. Bert was just beaten to the line by Thomas of Cambridge.

SOUTHERN VETS CC CHAMPS., LLOYD PARK, 5 FEB

This event has become less popular with Belgrave Vets over the last couple of years and the only one to brave the sticky mud and the hills of Lloyd Park was ... yes, you've guessed it, Charlie Walker.

Charlie ran very well, winning the bronze medal in the M60 race. He might have done even better had he not run off course when leading at the end of the second of the three lap course. He was running just behind the pack of leading Lady Vets and hadn't realised that they had turned off for their finish. Charlie lost a good forty or fifty metres and the lead. Should have kept your eyes on the course Charlie!

BVAF NATIONAL CC CHAMPS., BURNLEY, 7 MAR

It was an early Sunday morning start for the combined Belgrave/VAC party who made the long trip north to Burnley for this year's Vets National. A successful trip too, with Bob Treadwell winning the M40 race, silver medals for the Belgrave M60 team, and Bob Belmore a rival member of the winning Barnet squad.

On arrival, Townley Park fell somewhat short of the vision some had of beautiful north country moors. The start was a flat scrubby playing field alongside a dirty stream, then came a long, long, muddy climb of at least three quarters of a mile up to the edge of a council estate at the top of the surrounding hills. Down again, past a huge ugly factory, and then came the wade through a smelly stream to the finish. All this three times. However, the day was very well organised, the competition intense, and one wise old runner kindly reminded us that when the race was last held in the South the venue was Wormwood Scrubs!

With Laurie O'Hara missing from the Belgrave team it was Charlie Walker, in inspired form, who led the Belgrave M60's in the first race. Charlie finished 7th in his age category, an improvement from last year and even ahead of a tired looking Tony Stone. Strong runs from Bert Stroud and Pat Newell made up the scoring three with Arthur Bruce and Fred Paget freely offering advice from the side. Barnet had their new star, Ron Higgs, and did just enough to take gold, which of course was much commented upon afterwards by Bob Belmore.

Bob Treadwell had rested from the National at Parliament Hill the previous week in anticipation of the strong field and the demanding course. He found the long, slow climbs to his liking, reminiscent of several Continental hill races that had given him success in the past and suited to long striding runners with long hamstrings who are able to find the right breathing rhythm. (All age winners were built thus.) Bob got away on the first climb, and although always wary of the in form Brian Kirkwood from Scotland who finished ahead of him in the Inter-Counties, held on well for a great victory.

Charlie Dickinson hasn't got long hamstrings and was rather disappointed with 26th place after finishing 11th the previous year. The long drive as chauffeur may also have taken its toll.

With Maggie Statham, coached by Bob Belmore, and Steve Charlton also winning their races, it was a successful day for VAC and the South. The long drive home gave us a mixture of snoozing, stories of races from the past and more friendly Belgrave/Barnet banter.

"Don't worry, we'll have you lot in the relay".

"Why don't you rejoin us instead of running for that North London lot ? On second thoughts it would be a waste of time, we don't run a 'B' team !"

Well, perhaps not quite so friendly !

items.heading: Another successful season
items.summary: Leo Coy reviews the young athletes' cross-country season and their first year in the U13 Indoor Sportshall League.
items.text:
Another successful season

Another successful cross-country season has ended with good all round performances by all age group teams and some very good individual results.

The season got under way in October with a win for the Youths in the Surrey CC Relay. The event was held on the old Surrey AC relay course in Richmond Park.

Our HHH League performance was probably our best ever. We managed to get team or individual prizes in all groups as well as winning third overall for combined age groups. Simon Vella, Gavin Jones, John Wilson and Adam Jones all performed very well in each match.

In the Surrey League our combined Youths/Boys team had no opposition all year. Matthew Hillier won two races with Adam Jones and Gavin Mason winning the other two. This, with good back-up from the Boys, ensured that we won with ease. Tom Evans and Simon Alexander had great runs at Lloyd Park - they surprised some of the Youths and pushed them out of the scoring five! Unfortunately we will be in Division Two with the Seniors next year.

The County Championships saw mixed performances with the best result coming from Simon Vella, who came 2nd in the Middlesex Colts' race.

At the Southern, we finished our full quota of eight in the Boys' age group and the team were 20th. Simon Alexander had a good run to lead the team home in 51st place. The Youths team finished 7th overall, without Gavin or Stuart Booth. Matthew and Adam had excellent runs.

This year for the first time we participated in the Indoor Sportshall League for the U13 age group. The league was held over three matches and took place in large sports halls. The events consist of sprints, relays, paarlauf, plus throws and jumps. Each team is made up of six competitors and each can only do one individual event. Everybody takes part in the final relay.

The competition was fierce, with an excellent atmosphere at each venue. It is an exciting event which will continue to grow in popularity and will be an alternative to an easy winter for our young throwers, sprinters and jumpers.

We performed well throughout and won the final match at Cheam. Es Hassan, Andrew Hill, Duncan Thompson, Steve Taylor and Dwaine Patterson were selected to represent Surrey in the National Event.

Thanks to Chris. Knight, Billy Bull and Martin Milner for their help throughout the season and also thanks to the parents who supported us so well. I must not forget Steve Whorlow, for his role as acting team manager when I was delayed - I did have a long way to travel. Captains Toby, Marlon and Adam played their part all season during both training and competition.

Next season sees the start of the new age bands which will mean that most of our Youths will miss their second winter season in the age group and will become Juniors. Let us hope that they continue to improve together and become our Senior team of the future.

Leo Coy

items.heading: Step by step guide to Athletic Meetings
items.summary: Sue Porter describes how track and field officials get involved and what organising an athletics meeting involves, appealing for helpers.
items.text:
Step by step guide to Athletic Meetings

Everyone competes at athletic meetings, local leagues or national leagues and probably only notice the field and track officials in passing. They're those men and women in the navy jackets!

How do these officials get involved in the first place? Often it's as a parent helping out, holding tapes, collecting shot, even timekeeping. Then before they know it they're hooked and, having taken a straightforward test, become a Graded Official, the first step on the ladder to becoming Chief Track Judge, Referee or Timekeeper.

So now we have a band of officials, how do we proceed?

We first have to agree on a date to hold the meeting. This is a lot more difficult than you would expect or believe. With so many meetings held in the summer, tracks are booked up very early. And of course it's best not to clash with national or county events, or any of the established leagues.

Once the date has been sorted out then a timetable and list of events can be drawn up. Adverts for entries are placed in the magazines and circularised to other clubs in the area and then it's time to sit back and wait for the entries to come pouring in.

On the day itself, the most important concern is the weather. As long as the rain isn't too heavy, or the snow can be swept off the track and field areas, we are all systems go. Also, whether or not all officials and helpers manage to park their cars close enough to the track to haul their bags of wet gear and other equipment; and whether the refreshments are available throughout the meeting. Officials work best on sweet tea and ginger biscuits.

After a successful meeting you'd think it would be an easy matter to lock up and return all the equipment to the rightful places. But there's always some items of kit to return to owners - if you can find them. One starter, who shall remain nameless, was without his red jacket - heaven forbid - for some months. Don't ask how he managed to be an official starter without it.

So then it's time to retire, battered and shattered and mentally bereft, to go through the results and send out the medals, etc., not collected. Oh well! Leave that 'til tomorrow ... Tomorrow's another day - and next week's another meeting ...

Easy isn't it? You too can help, you really can. You're only a 'phone call away from a fun-filled summer officiating for Belgrave Harriers.

Sue Porter (Club Starter & General Secretary)

• Competing in the Phoenix Races at Brighton on 8th November, Adam Jones placed 3rd in the Youths 4k event in 12:10 while James Drake was 5th in the Boys race in 10:16.

• Marlon Dickson became a Surrey Champion early in the year when he won the indoor 60m in 7.8 at Crystal Palace on Feb 21st.

• The Mini-Marathon trials to determine who would represent their boroughs in the young athletes races on London Marathon day gave two Belgravians a chance to show their paces. Ben Hamill won his race at Richmond while the Wandsworth event saw Marlon Anderson fill a similar position.

• In the Middlesex Championships Simon Vella was 2nd in the Colts age group with 12:00 and John Wilson was 13th Boy in 15:45. The Kent Championships saw Nigel Whorlow come home 34th and in Sussex, Gavin Jones was 9th in 15:07. No fewer than eight of our lads were selected to represent their counties in the Inter-Counties event.

items.text:
Points Competition 1992/93

The cross-country points competition was well supported by our youngsters with no fewer than 39 runners having turned out for the eight designated points races by the time the winter was over. In fact it was attendance at the matches which was the most important part of the competition, with place points only being brought into the equation where runners had made the same number of appearances. Interestingly enough, only one Boy managed to get to every single event and would you believe it, he is the one who lives furthest away - Nigel Whorlow of Folkestone!

Well done to all who took part.

items.heading: A Team Manager's DREAM
items.summary: Harry Porter's profile of Ladies' Captain Jacinta Moore (née Coppinger): her running since joining from Dublin in 1985, her GRE Cup 3,000m win at Kingston in 1987, her marriage and the birth of daughter Cliona.
items.text:
Harry Porter writes about Jacinta Moore née Coppinger, one of our Ladies' Captains, whom he describes as

A Team Manager's DREAM

I first met Jacinta in November 1985, just after the cross-country season had started. It was my second season as Ladies Team Manager, having succeeded Derek Jones after his five year stint. Since that time Jacinta has competed on the Road, Country and Track, making over 150 appearances in the Belgrave team despite a break of some months due to muscle injury and extensive physiotherapy.

Jacinta's first appearance for Belgrave was at the Surrey Women's Cross Country League Meeting at Ewell Court, just before Christmas 1985. She had only recently come to England from her native Dublin and had joined us soon after her arrival. That first season started with a good first run, 23rd, and she went on to finish the winter in 13th. Not bad at all for a first attempt.

She had originally wanted to run longer distances and even now enjoys an occasional half-marathon. In fact she came second to Leslie Watson in the Welwyn 20 mile road race in February 1985 and in 1990 ran alongside the likes of Greta Weitz and Rosa Mota in the Women's Great London Run over 10k where she finished a creditable 21st in 38:34. That 10k was a pretty good performance when you consider that the day before she had run in the Hertford County Road Relays where her second-claim team had placed 2nd.

Representing Hertfordshire on numerous occasions over both Country and Track, Jacinta's best result was a fourth position in the County Cross Country Championships of 1988 and she has run for that county in the Southern and National Inter-Counties events. On the track she was silver medallist in the Herts. County Championships 3,000m for two consecutive years from 1988, running 10:40 both times.

Having lived in Surrey for the last two years, Jacinta now has Surrey qualifications and in 1992 ran the in the County 10k Road Championships when the Belgrave Ladies were second team. The team went on to win the first ever Women's Surrey Road League in the summer of 1992.

As well as track and cross-country, Jacinta also enjoys the longer relays, and in particular the now defunct 25 x 1 mile relay held at the end of the track season. She competed in the race every year until the last in 1989. However, since 1988 the Ladies have also taken part in the Ostende Relays. The distances in this event vary from 100m to 600m and Jacinta has run a 600m leg ever since the team first ventured onto the Continent. She was also a member of the Southern Women's 3 x 800m gold medal winning team in 1987, along with Jacqui Smiter and Jackie Stone.

Jacinta has been Track Captain since 1986 when she saw the team finish 7th in their first season in the Southern Women's League Division 2, narrowly missing promotion direct to Division 1. And in 1987 she led Belgrave into the semi-final of the GRE Cup, the only Division 2 team to have achieved that status since 1984.

Jacinta considers that her most memorable day was the Melbourne Trophy International match at Crystal Palace in September 1987, where she came 3rd in the mile in 5:16.86. However, I would have to disagree, remembering her 4th place in the Surrey Women's Cross Country League match at Ewell Court, November 1990. But then again, from the spectators point of view, her 3,000m in that GRE Cup semi-final qualifier at Kingston in June 1987 takes some beating.

She had gone out hard in front, leading the race for the first three laps. The rest of the pack, after recovering from the shock, gradually managed to pull her back and the Belgravian dropped to 4th position, to all intents and purposes, spent. But not so, because 400 metres from the finish she changed gear and went for the front again, making up over 30 metres in the last lap. To roaring and screaming from Belgrave teammates she surged through at the line to finish 1st. The whole field crossed the line within 5 metres. It was a thrilling race and she had gained six valuable points which took the team into the semi-finals for 1987. Jacinta had knocked a massive 1 minute off her personal best at the beginning of that season and a further 13 seconds had come off just two weeks previously. What a tremendous performance and what a memorable day for the whole team.

Apart from having competed for Belgrave and Hertfordshire, Jacinta also enters many road races, both here and in Eire. In 1991 she won the Limerick 5 miles road title, and she also took the Billericay 9 miles with 57:20.

However, life changed drastically and irrevocably for Jacinta in that year. She met her future husband Michael after an unfortunate accident with wet paint - you will have to ask Jacinta for the full story - my lips are sealed. But the incident did prove very fortunate for the couple who married towards the end of 1991, when Sue and myself were privileged to attend on behalf of the Club. The wedding was held on a beautiful sunny day at a quiet country church beside the shimmering waters of a lough.

At a photocall afterwards, the neat group of Michael, his parents and two brothers were swamped when the photographer innocently called for the bride and her family. Jacinta's parents, her eleven brothers and sisters and their wives and children surged into view - the photographer needed a wide angle lens to cope with this sitting!

"It was a quiet year," says Jacinta.

In June 1992 Jacinta spread the glad tidings that she was pregnant, and her daughter Cliona was born on 1st February this year. Jacinta had raced in the Wimbledon 5k in early December, just eight weeks before the baby's arrival, and was back in action in the very last cross-country race of the season, which included the Belgrave Championships, on March 13th. Almost a Liz McColgan!

Many team managers would dream of having a Jacinta in their team. She is wholly committed to her club where, for her, events takes precedence over any other competition. She is one of those rare people who are able to get that little bit extra from people when that little bit extra can make all the difference. A good motivator without a doubt, the Belgrave Women's Section is so much the better for her presence.

For everything you have achieved for us, Jacinta, we all thank you. Well done - and here's to the future too.

Harry Porter

items.heading: Thanks from Harry P
items.summary: Ladies Team Manager Harry Porter congratulates the women on their winter season, including the Surrey League Division 2 title and Surrey road championship trophies.
items.text:
Thanks from Harry P

As Ladies Team Manager, I would like to congratulate the Ladies for their very successful season over the country and road this winter, following their achievement in winning the first Surrey Women's Summer Road League in 1992.

Over the winter of 1992/93 the women turned in tremendous performances to win the Surrey Cross Country League Division 2 by a huge margin and gain promotion to Division 1. Although down on numbers for the Winter Road League, they still managed to come a creditable 3rd.

In the 5k and 10k Surrey Road Championships our Ladies took both trophies and in the longer race we won with the minimum score - our team placing 1st, 2nd and 3rd in the Surrey race and 2nd, 3rd and 4th overall.

Many congratulations. Well done! Let's hope that this sparkling winter can transfer onto the track for equally good performances in the Southern Women's T&F League and Surrey Summer Road League.

As well as the good performances, I would like to thank my Assistant Team Manager, Cynthia James, and travelling official, Derek Jones, for their sterling efforts on our behalf.

Harry Porter

items.heading: A little depleted
items.summary: Carl Lawton's walking section round-up of a thin winter, with walkers away, injured or off form, and news of a vets' track league and a possible ladies team.
items.text:
A little depleted

The winter season did not produce much in the way of success. We still rely on the mature walkers and with the absence of Doug Fotheringham and John Dunsford on a three month jaunt to foreign parts and competing in the Oceanic Games, we have been a little depleted. To add to our woe Paul King had a disagreement with a car (who said "Not again!") so he has been off the road since January. Pat Duncan achieved a performance that has taken him 30 years - he actually beat Ray Middleton in a race. However, Ray will probably admit to being a little off form.

During the next few months there is the chance to join in with the track and field side competing in the vets. league over 2k. Those interested please see fixture card. It is only two over 40s and one over 50 to score but there will be space for non-scorers.

Karen Barker has been off the road for a while but now having given birth to twins, both girls, she may soon be out and about again. To give her some incentive Gill Brackpool has started training again and so there is the possibility of having a ladies team out.

Carl Lawton

LONDON POSTAL REGION 10k, BLACKHEATH, 6 SEP

Lawton was in the frame as the Bels. backed him up to a rare team triumph. Mike Scamell was in particular having a good month, and able to break the paternal pattern now required of Mike the 'Dad.'

BELGRAVE 3k TRACK CHAMPS, BATTERSEA PARK, 7 SEP

The following day, on a nearly deserted Battersea track, a World and Commonwealth Champion had a spin in Bels. colours and duly won the race if not the Club Championship.

Simon Baker, about to return to Oz, two hours later in fact, was staying with Paul Warburton who strong-armed the Victorian into his first effort since the Olympic 50k!

Back to Blackheath for another Bels. win; this time in the form of John Hall in his Min of Ag. colours, making light of the undulating course. He was followed by the rarely seen shape of John Llewellin, now working in deepest Kent.

BERT ANGELL 7m, HENDON, 13 SEP

Bels. on a roll decided to cash in at Hendon where Lawton was at the finish long before his team mates Scamell and Warburton who nonetheless had better than average efforts.

This must have been the smallest ever field for this event and unless numbers generally increase must spell the end.

1, D.Baxter (Steyning) 40:55; 2, C.Lawton (Belgrave) 43:20; 3, D.Fotheringham 44:22; 4, P.King 45:30; 8 finished.

CAMBRIDGE H WINTER LEAGUE 10k, BEXLEY, 24 OCT

Excuse No. 63! the 'off' found at least four of the field tying up their laces. Reason? The gun at these races is synchronised with two other 'starts': when these go - everyone does, regardless of previously announced start times. Needless to say, two of the tardy had mixed fortunes. Paul Warburton called it quits trying to make up lost ground, while Surrey's Chris Cheeseman passed the entire field bar one: the organiser, Noel Carmody. (Are you trying to say something, Ed.?)

1, N.Carmody (Cambridge H) 46:54; 2, C.Cheeseman (Surrey WC) 47:12; 3, S.Uttley (Ilford) 49:47; ... 7, D.Fotheringham 55:03; 8, P.King 56:13.

ENFIELD OPEN 7m, 14 NOV

This course, over the years, has decreased in scope while traffic on the surrounding roads of the Q.E. Stadium has grown, which while making for a traffic free environment, now presents new hazards: footballs and toddlers; the former flying off the adjacent pitches, the latter let off the leash by unsuspecting parents - into the path of 8 mile an hour walkers.

Not that this made any difference to Steyning's Darrell Stone, or for that matter to a relatively replete Belgrave team, who did well to finish in the frame, and avoid obstacles!

The Belgrave '7' almost repeated the performance only this time it was Julie Drake and John Hall. John, probably not having forgotten the previous occasion, put all his effort in to hold off Julie and break away for a clear win.

The turn-out was slightly down on last year and only three teams closed in, thus giving Basingstoke a place in the frame.

SOUTHERN RWA & LONDON CHAMPS, CRYSTAL PALACE, 6 FEB

Poor John Keown! The Belgrave stalwart and sometime Southern Area Secretary was led a merry dance by the Sports Council who promised financial returns in exchange for the championships being shifted from the traditional venue of Battersea Park to the park paths surrounding the National Sporting Centre.

Not only did the money never appear, but John and Mick and Barbara Marshall had to battle all kinds of bureaucratic blunders to get the races staged at all.

Nor did the date appeal to some. At least one south coast club whose fixture had always been on the first Saturday in February, complained bitterly in print about the choice of this date for the championships, which now incorporate three races in one: the 'Garnet' Cup for novices is also part of the programme.

In the event, an under strength Belgrave team missed out on London medals for the first time in living memory, despite a back to some-kind-of-form effort from Carl Lawton, who made light work of the twists and turns of the traffic free course, and a sterling effort in the women's 5k from Sue Porter who secured a London Champs. bronze.

MIDDLESEX, BUCKS & HERTS 10m CHAMPS., ENFIELD 28 FEB

Four in a row for John Hall who may hold some kind of enviable record for being the closest competing athlete in Great Britain to the start line of an official race. Can anyone do better than 160 metres from front door to start line?

On a bitter, sleet ridden day, our man from the ministry was well served by his thermal tights, eventually leading both Middlesex and Belgrave to an easy win.

Middlesex teams: 1, Belgrave.

NATIONAL 20k CHAMPS./ WORLD CUP TRIALS, CARDIFF, 14 MAR

Held on an exciting 20 lap circuit of 500metres up and 500 metres back on the same stretch of road, this must pose the question of where British walking is going. Only 50 or so finished; it was supposed to be a trial but did not really come up with a satisfactory result. The one positive outcome was that only four of the first twenty were vets. and the course was at least in pleasant surroundings and completely traffic free.

This National is usually held in May and on a Saturday so one must ask if the walkers did not turn out because of these changes.

Belgrave began the year on the right foot by starting a team and finishing one, just.

You will notice that for the first time in many a year we have listed our Club Coaches on the summer fixture card. And of course, what is the obvious thing that happens? - we leave someone out. Sorry Ray! Let us make amends by declaring that Ray Hall, coaching walking, will be in attendance at Battersea Park.

We understand that Gordon Doubleday has spent a little time in hospital where he has been found to be diabetic. However, he is now back home and we hope that his complaint is not troubling him too much.

There, in the March issue of CBI News, sharing a page with an article on "World Development Awards" and another describing how British managers should be equipped to do business in Japan, was a startlingly different advert. "Belgrave Harriers - UK champions" it was headed, and showed the well-known Mark Shearman colour photograph of John Regis passing the baton to Jon Ridgeon that graced the cover of our own magazine a few issues back. The advertisement was the idea of Bill Laws, hoping to find a UK firm for whom we could do promotional work while in Hungary for the European Clubs Cup Final, and of course also aiming at potential sponsors. Let's hope that the calculating mind of some captain of industry is grabbed by the idea, for we are currently one of the very few top clubs without a sponsor of any kind.
