items.heading: The Record Breaker
items.summary: Alan Mead's eyewitness recollection, as a 16-year-old fan, of Stan Vickers breaking George Larner's 1904 UK 2 miles walk record with 13:02.4 against Ken Matthews at the 1960 AAA Championships at the White City, with notes on the 1960 Rome and 1964 Tokyo Olympic walks.
items.text:
The Record Breaker

I had set out hours ago, having walked to the bus-stop at the Malden Roundabout and then ridden the number 72 route all the way to Shepherd's Bush, dispatching a "hay stack" of corned beef and tomato sandwiches long before crossing the river at Hammersmith. There was a great confluence of athletics fans in Wood Lane. Thousands, like me, were trekking up from the "Bush", and hordes poured out of the tube station. All had come to the White City to be at the 1960 AAA Championships and watch the likes of Peter Radford, Milkha Singh and Gordon Pirie go through their paces in preparation for the forthcoming Rome Olympics.

Belgrave had some pretty good sprinters and middle-distance men in those far off days and I was keen to see them in action but in 1960 the Belgrave Walking Section was supreme. Walking Secretary Jack Goswell was able to deploy some half a dozen internationals in team races and they had swept all before them - the Leicester '20', RWA '20', RWA '50' - all had featured 'BELGRAVE H' at the top of the result sheet. This day was going to give me the chance to see one of those heroes, Stan Vickers, in combat with his Midland rival Ken Matthews of Royal Sutton Coldfield. Both were to duel in the walker's sprint - the 2 miles. Both were in superb form and the likelihood was that the UK record of 13:11.4, set 56 years earlier on 13th July 1904 by George E. Larner, was going to go.

High up on the concrete terracing of that draughty stadium, now long gone, I had a bird's-eye view of the arena. The dull red clay track contrasted with the surrounding grass oval of the greyhound-racing circuit that separated the fans from the competitors. No digital results display-screen in 1960 of course, but a huge white results board and a large clock with a sweep second hand by which one could judge the athletes' progress versus the record book.

The three weeks before the event had already seen some astounding 2 mile walk times. At Motspur Park in the Southern Champs. Stan had won in his best ever time of 13:31.8, beating his own championship best by 17 seconds. On the same day Matthews had taken the Midland title, also in a championship best, with 13:36. Just a few days later in a club match against the Stock Exchange at Battersea the Belgravian had gone faster still with 13:26.4 and then, the very next Saturday, on Peterborough's grass track, Ken and Stan clashed in an invitation race where the latter confidently sprinted to victory and actually equalled Larner's 1904 record. Again at Battersea, on the Wednesday night preceding the AAA, the record withstood another assault as Vickers scorched to a time just one fifth of a second slower. Surely that time would crumble today.

Eighteen men faced the starter and the four East Germans, Lindner, Hildebrand, Adolph and Pathus, together with the Sikhs Zora and Adjit Singh, made it a truly international field. Stan was not the only Belgravian in the line-up as Eric Hall was also hoping to impress.

The start was unbelievably fast. At the gun Zora Singh tore into the lead and after a single circuit the timekeepers logged lap one at 1:34.3 - that's 12:34 pace! Matthews and Vickers were in tow and then came Colin Williams, Adjit Singh and Lindner. But the inevitable happened, Zora had thrown caution to the winds with his effort and after half a mile the judges pulled him out, a fate that soon befell his fellow countryman and two of the Germans. Now it was the powerful Matthews blasting along at the front with Vickers so close behind him that they were later described as "siamese twins".

The mile came up - 6:30.2 - had such a time ever been recorded before? Williams was now in trouble some 15 seconds behind and was soon to be swept up by Lindner and Hall. It was obvious that the burly Sutton Coldfield man was out to avenge that defeat of the previous week but how on earth could he keep such a pace going. One of these two must crack soon.

Further laps of 99 to 100 seconds unreeled - one and a half miles in 9:51.4. I can't remember a walk before or since causing such an uproar from the crowd. Still only one yard covered the two protagonists as the strident clangour of the last lap bell cut through the cheers. Ken Matthews needed just one more lap in 1:40.5 to take the record but something in the angular frame of the man in his wake foretold of more drama to come.

Stan suddenly veered out and round the Midlander in an all-out heel and toe sprint. For an instant Matthews seemed stunned before he too released every remaining spark of energy left in his body. Vickers had taken twenty yards by the back straight and as the final turn was approached, spectators were torn between the vision of Ken Matthews desperately trying to get back into contention, Stan Vickers racing towards the finish line, and that giant second-hand on the result board, sweeping inexorably on towards the top of the clock and the 13 minute mark. Tumultuous cheers reached an even greater volume as the Belgrave Harrier crossed the line. He had clearly smashed the record and for an instant it seemed that he might have even gone under 13 minutes. Within a short while it was announced that Larner's time had been beaten by 9 seconds and that Matthews too had gone inside the old mark.

1, S.E.Vickers (Belgrave) 13:02.4 (UK and AAA National Record); 2, K.J.Matthews (Royal Sutton Coldfield) 13:09.6; 3, D.Lindner (E.Germany); 4, E.W.Hall (Belgrave) 13:51.8.

It's a sobering thought that Stan's time was worth around 12:09 for the modern-day equivalent of the race - 3,000 metres.

That day at the White City was, of course, just a landmark on the road to greater glory for several of the competitors. In the sweltering heat of the Rome Olympics where just about every British distance athlete performed well below par, Stan became the 20 kilometre Walk bronze medallist in 1 hour 34 minutes and 57 seconds, 49 seconds behind the great Soviet Champion Golubnichiy. At the half-way point Stan had passed a badly suffering Ken Matthews who commanded a 19 second lead at one stage, only to falter in the conditions and later require hospital treatment. Eric Hall also posted an excellent performance in that Rome race, coming home 10th. Ken's day of Olympic triumph came four years later at the Tokyo Games when it was his turn to win gold with Lindner 2nd.

But back on that July Saturday evening in 1960 it just remained for a 16 year old Belgravian to walk back to Shepherd's Bush and wait for the bus, head a-buzzing with the excitement of seeing a fellow Club member setting a UK record.

Alan Mead

items.heading: Seven go to Guernsey
items.summary: Terry Lawton's light-hearted account of seven Belgrave runners' Easter racing trip to Guernsey: a six mile road race, five miles cross country, a two mile cross country relay and a half-marathon in which Helen Maskrey won the ladies' prize and overall title.
items.text:
Seven go to Guernsey

How did you spend Easter this year? Seven of us went to Guernsey for four days of racing.

We met at Gatwick, except for 'Wassie', who must have known something was up because we had a four hour delay (he went from Heathrow). Don also must have known something, having booked for a later flight but arriving two hours before us.

"Just smell that sea air," said Fred, to which Michelin-man Ross replied, "Stuff the sea air - where's our hotel?"

Helen went for a drive and promptly got lost due to a lack of signposts and it wasn't long before the rest of us were in similar trouble. We only had to travel three miles to book in for our races but returned after an hour having driven nineteen miles and still not found the place to register. Why no signposts? Something to do with confusing the enemy in the last war!

Six mile road race.

Good Friday dawned, grey, misty and miserable. We left for the race armed with excuses in true Belgravian tradition. Fred reminded us that he was getting over an injury, "so I'll be coach". 'Michelin' was complaining about his achilles problems while Carl, who hadn't actually run for a year, decided to stay behind and do some shopping.

Wiser than yesterday we elected 'Squaddie' Don as navigator, "Cos he's a trained soldier and leader of men," said 'Coach'. It was a good choice and we arrived on time.

The course was billed as undulating but could have been considered mountainous.

"What time are you expecting to run it in, 'Squaddie'?" I asked.

"Oh! about 38 minutes. Do you want to follow me?"

"Great, thanks," I said, and then he promptly blasted home in 36 minutes, forcing 'Michelin' and I to run 12:30 for the first two miles. We later seized on this as one of our excuses for 'blowing up'.

Results: Don 36:10, Helen 36:40 (4th lady), 'Wassie' 38:12, Terry 42:24, Ross 44:55.

Five miles cross country

Saturday arrived wet and windy. Carl decided that today he would look after the kit and 'Coach', who had seen a lady in blue shorts, suddenly forgot all about his injury and in chasing her had the most enjoyable run of the day!

"Hey! Carl. How did my dry kit get wet?"

"I don't know. It must have been wet when you gave it to me."

'Coach', always one to drop someone else in it, revealed the truth: "He was sitting on it".

Results: Don 29:32, Helen 30:24 (pb for this course and 3rd lady overall), 'Wassie' 31:34, Terry 32:34, Ross 35:10.

Two mile cross country relay

The course for Sunday's race was muddy, hilly and very wet. Carl stayed in the hotel to rest from the exertion of carrying my wet kit! Don ran his heart out and had to sit down afterwards to recuperate. It was the first time he had rested all week. Helen ran hard, looked cool and actually enjoyed it. She taunted me as I approached the finish: "Where's that famous sprint now?" So I kicked and got a pb. Thanks 'Mummy Bunny'. 'Michelin' left his shoes in the mud and finished in his socks - well actually they were mine. 'Wassie' ran for the 'Stragglers' but the Bels team beat them.

'Coach' advised us that the team would probably be at their peak in September but I thought I ran well and wasn't the only one - "Even 'Wassie' with his sun-lamp and bull-worker couldn't beat rising star Terry," said 'Squaddie'.

'Wassie' was seen throwing muddy old socks into the hedge but they were later rescued by 'Squaddie' to take home for Keith Duckett, although Helen quipped that they would't be old enough for him.

Results: Don 12:31, Helen 12:56 (pb and fastest lady), Terry 14:00, 'Wassie' 14:02, Ross 15:28.

Half-Marathon

Our worst fears were met as we gathered for the start of the half-marathon. The wind was so strong that all thoughts of pbs. evaporated. 'Michelin' bravely offered to run in place of our gallant 'Squaddie' who lay sick in bed with beads of perspiration on his forehead, having given all for the Bels. the day before.

For Helen there was a dilemma. She was joint leader overall, so should she now lead from the start or sit behind her rivals and then pounce at the end. Urged on by 'Coach' she determinedly led from the gun. After a few miles she was caught by a local male runner who patronisingly said, "stay with me luv and I'll get you round". Well, it was like a red rag to a bull. Our Helen dropped the foolish man when he hesitated at the first waterhole. "Eat dirt, sucker," she muttered.

At the half-way turn-around she passed me with a cheery call, her rivals now 200 metres behind. Storming home she took the first ladies prize, won the ladies' overall title and even had the energy to join 'Squaddie', who had now risen from his sick-bed, to cheer the rest of us over the line.

Results: Helen 1:24, 'Wassie' 1:27:25, Terry 1:39:10, Ross 1:52:03 ('Boofer' please note).

A great time. Why not join us next year?

Terry Lawton

The seven were John Wasbrough, Terry Lawton, Helen Maskrey, Don Anderson, Carl Cross, Fred Paget and Ross Martin.

items.summary: Archive photo of the finish of the half-mile handicap at a Belgrave Harriers meeting at Battersea Park in May 1929, won by Tom Pritchard, with Charlie Jones's recollections.
items.text:
May 1929

It's May 1929 and the crowds have again turned out in force to watch an athletic meeting put on at Battersea Park Athletic Track by the Belgrave Harriers. The half-mile handicap was a close affair up front with Tom Pritchard just triumphing over Alf Club of Kent A.C., and T.C. "Charlie" Jones in 3rd place. All three were well clear of Ernie Duffett and Joe Coleman who can be seen in the distance and the winning time was 1 minute 59 and 4-5th seconds. The photograph appeared on the back page of a subsequent "Daily Mirror" and Charlie Jones has kept his copy of the picture safe these 64 years since. Charlie recalls that the first meeting he ever saw was in 1921, also at Battersea, when Micky Pyer won a mile championship race. In those days there was a putting green where the car park now is, and for big meetings the Club used to get permission to erect a marquee on it for changing facilities. Now that we have re-published the photo' it will go into Belgrave's growing archive of such items, currently looked after by Clive Shippen.

items.summary: Letter to Derek Crookes from Stan Scarsbrook, an 84-year-old former Surrey AC runner living in Scotland, recalling his career and Belgrave contemporaries, printed under the letters heading "Write on!".
items.text:
Write on!

Enjoyed all of it

The following was received by Derek Crookes as a result of an enquiry from an old worthy of Surrey AC who wondered what had happened to his Club. As a Life Member of Surrey, his name has been added to our mailing list.

Dear Mr. Crookes,
Thank you for giving my grandson the information regarding Surrey AC. I have been in Scotland for 19 years. I still follow athletics and I wondered what had happened.
I am 84 and still take an active part in sport, playing golf now and again. I have won the Senior Championship twice and even had a "hole in one".
I always think of the good times I had when running and enjoyed all of it - the friendships with other athletes and the good competitions we had. I knew A. Penny, B. Footer and C. Carter of Belgrave well. I had a lucky career - Sussex 3 miles champion, Empire Games steeplechase and lots of other races. I was an Army runner also.
I remember Mr. Vowles very well. Surrey AC made me a Life Member in 1935.
I wish your club all the very best and hope you win more trophies.
My best regards to A. Penny and any of the old Belgrave Lads.
Stan Scarsbrook, Peeblesshire.

items.summary: Letter from Doris M. Dean taking ARM to task over the November 1992 article on E.F. Vowles of Surrey Athletic Club, saying Vowles would have been horrified at the 1982 amalgamation with Belgrave.
items.text:
... But we are taken to task

Dear Editors,
It was a pleasure to receive the November '92 issue of "The Belgravian" and congratulations on a very informative and interesting magazine.
As you can imagine, being an old stalwart of Surrey Athletic Club, I was most interested in your article regarding Mr. E.F. Vowles - 'The Grand Old Man of Athletics', but I would take ARM to task when he states at the end of the article that "were Mr. Vowles alive today he would be proud of the contribution his clubmen have made in forming part of a team ... etc., etc."
'V' would have been horrified to think his members would ever contemplate being anything other than Surrey AC. He breathed and lived Surrey Athletic Club, it was his baby, his family and his life - sometimes to the exclusion of his own family.
He died in impoverished circumstances in his 95th year, having given his money and health to athletics over many years and I for one am more than pleased that he was not alive in August 1982 when members of that era decided to amalgamate with the Belgrave Harriers.
I knew Mr. Vowles very well and visited him up to the time of his death and am still in touch with his family, so I think I can safely say I knew how he felt about Surrey Athletic Club and I am sorry that ARM did not finish his excellent article after "his eightieth year". (full-stop)
Doris M. Dean (Mrs), Merton Park

items.heading: 'Doub' recalls '42
items.summary: Letter from Gordon Doubleday recalling his wartime years: evacuation to Exeter, running for Exeter H., the 1942 Poly Marathon, Syd Ring's London-Brighton relay mishap, and Harry Parker producing The Belgravian in wartime.
items.text:
'Doub' recalls '42

Dear Editors,
As usual I enjoyed my visit to Wimbledon for the Club's Open Walk. Carl gave me "Something to read on the train," which, of course, was "The Belgravian".
Under the title "50 Years Ago" I see my return to London mentioned. For those not around those 50 years ago perhaps I'd better explain.
When WW2 broke out (Sep'39) my firm evacuated my wife, baby daughter and myself to Exeter where we had an emergency lab. in case our London premises (Bishopsgate) got "bombed" - which they did. When Exeter was "bombed" (April '42) we were moved back to London.
I joined Exeter H. There was little competition but we were allowed as guest runners in events held by University College of the S.W. and St. Lukes Teacher Training College. Both of these are now part of Exeter University. I used to try and manage a Saturday run and a midweek one.
The day I came back to London was the 1,000th day of the war - also in time to enter the Poly Marathon. I had gained standard medals (3 1/2 hrs) in the '38 and '39 events from Windsor to the Poly track at Chiswick. The war time Polys were held on the four lap course from Chiswick. In 1942 they decided to award medals on the basis of one for every six entrants (there were 90). I had the joy of picking off a few stragglers on the last lap to finish 15th - the last of the medal winners!
As mentioned club mate Syd Ring was second. Syd was very meticulous regarding his running. He once did the stage on the London-Brighton Relay which included the level crossing at Crawley. He looked up time tables and worked out that if things went as planned the gates would be open when he was due. Unfortunately, as he approached the gates they closed for an unscheduled goods train, so he had to use the pedestrian subway. He took it all very calmly.
Back to myself! When the war began I had settled down as Hon. Editor of "The Belgravian", but, being away from London, was unable to continue. Luckily our Asst Hon. Secretary Harry Parker not only produced wartime Belgravians, but summer and winter fixture lists. These were condensed onto postcards - in any case newsprint was hard to come by, but Harry managed it. After the war Harry became President of the E.C.C.U. but, sadly, died during his term of office. On my return to London I was able to help Harry with "The Belgravian". We tried to get the mag. to all members, especially those on active service abroad.
Gordon Doubleday, Bath

Alf would have been delighted

Dear Editors,
Thank you very much indeed for sending me a copy of "The Belgravian". It was interesting to see what it had grown into - most impressive. Alf would have been delighted with it.
I have kept in touch with some of his contemporaries, though sadly, numbers are dwindling. Win Martin Shepherd writes every Christmas to tell me the year's news and I appreciate her letters.
It's good to know that the Club continues to do well.
With all best wishes for many further successes.
Nancy Harley, Uxbridge

items.heading: One track mind
items.summary: Poem "One-Track Mind" by Ernest Obeng, from his Runner's Primer of Poetry, in which a partner complains about a runner's obsession.
items.text:
One track mind

- a Runner's Primer of Poetry by Ernest Obeng

One-Track Mind

"You've got a one-track mind," she said.
"You're always on the run.
Why don't you stop and use your head.
There are other kinds of fun.
I don't know why you have to wake
the household up at dawn
to jog for miles to sweat and ache,
and come home looking drawn.
Why don't you use your energy
on something else for once.
Just face up to reality
and give the world a chance.
When you get injured or don't win,
you take it out on us,
pretend you hold your feelings in
but love to have us fuss.
What pleasant evenings we spend;
you're either fast asleep
Or trying out the latest trend
That's hit the athlete's heap.
I'd love to sit and talk instead,
but then you have the knack
of using anything I've said
to talk some more of track.
You've got a one-track mind," she moaned.
Before she'd said some more,
I'd put my shoes on, tied my lace,
and jogged out through the door.

Published with the Ernie's kind permission

items.summary: Arthur Bruce's recollection of the 1948 athletics year: Wooderson's National cross country win over Vic Blowfield with Belgrave taking the team title, the London to Brighton Relay, the AAA Championships, the London Olympic Games day by day, and Belgrave's Olympians (Harry Churcher, Bill Nankeville, Bill Lucas, Etienne Gailly) and season, illustrated with a 1948 Elliman Athletic Rub advert, the Olympic programme cover and emblem, and an Ed. Lacey photo of Len Herbert and Bill Lucas.
items.text:
1948 by Arthur Bruce

1948! A year that conjures up pictures of titanic struggles climaxing in the first Post War Olympic Games in austerity ridden Britain with eager athletes deprived of Olympic competition since 1936, anxious to prove themselves. Arthur Bruce continues his tales of athletics from the post-war years.

After two post war seasons a pattern of World Athletics had solidified. And when the Games were ushered in on Friday 30th July 1948 at the newly laid track at Wembley Stadium, armed with our daily shilling (5p) programme, we were geared for a feast of athletics.

Wooderson's "National"

The British winter season that had preceded the Olympics had produced a number of post war stars to which had been added Sydney Wooderson, who after a magnificent track season of 1946 had professed his intention to finish his career by attempting to win the National Cross Country title.

Starting with an exploratory season in 1947, he entered 1948 with his running programme geared to the National in March at Graves Park, Sheffield. He achieved his objective after a tremendous struggle with our own Vic Blowfield, only taking the lead in the finishing funnel. Belgrave won the team race with 154 points beating their conquerors of 1947, Sutton Harriers by 20 points. The Bels scoring six were home in 57 places. Wooderson's subsequent performance in the International at Reading was disappointing, and coupled with the English team being comfortably beaten by the Belgians who were led by surprise winner, Jean Doms. For Wooderson it was the end of a brilliant career dating back to his public school mile win in the early 'thirties.

The year progressed to a short road relay season climaxing in April with the classic London to Brighton Relay which produced another great club struggle, with Bill Lucas taking Belgrave into the lead over Birchfield on the last stage into Brighton.

The track season

The track season was of course organised along simpler lines than today, with only the British Games and Inter-Counties at Whitsun weekend to interrupt the progression of County and District leading to the AAA Championships and selection for the Olympic Games held in the first week of July.

The principal talking points in early season were the hopes of McDonald Bailey, the Trinidadian born sprinter who had elected to run for Britain and who had shown such good form since 1946. This year, however, he was plagued with injuries and confronted by a new star. Alastair McCorquadale arrived suddenly on the sprinting scene, beating Bailey in the Kinnaird Trophy meeting. The other major talking point concerned Roger Bannister, the new Oxford discovery, who had been a surprise inter-varsity mile winner in 1947. Bannister wisely had turned down any thought of running in the 1948 Games, preferring to work to a long term plan for 1952 and Helsinki.

The AAA Championships proved to be as exciting as predicted. The 100yds provided a win for John Treloar the Australian sprint hope who just edged out McCorquadale and Bailey. McCorquadale returned to win the 220yds. Another Australian prodigy, Morris Curotta, won the 440yds from the best Britain could offer. The 880yds, probably the finest race of the Championships, seemed to be a struggle between Arthur Wint and the visiting New Zealand Champion Doug Harris until a few yards from the tape when both were overwhelmed by John Parlett's late surge. Bill Nankeville (Belgrave) gained the first of his four 1 mile titles with Roger Bannister in his Championship debut, in 5th place.

Other titles to go abroad were the 3 miles won by Wooderson's old rival Willie Slykhuis, the Dutch star, and the High and Long jumps to visiting Australian Olympians. The most promising performance from Britain's point of view was the win by the 18 year old schoolboy J.Burrell in the 120yds hurdles, beating several established stars. One could say that the British Olympic team possessed a number of possible winners while the opposition was difficult to gauge.

The "Games"

The Olympic Games were four weeks later, with 53 Nations providing 815 athletes. They were without Germany, Japan, Russia and most of the African Continent - a compact affair but of high quality nevertheless.

The opening day revealed the strength of the American team, especially in the sprints, 800 metres and 400 metre hurdles, with Britain's sprinters and middle distance runners also qualifying. The climax of the day was the revelation of the Games, Lt. Emil Zatopek of the Czech Army who demolished the field in the 10,000 metres, winning by over three-quarters of a minute and breaking the legend of the Finnish runners in this event, a distance they had dominated for over twenty years.

Day two, Saturday July 31st, threw up a surprise winner in the 100 metres. Gold medallist was the American third string Harrison Dillard, in reality a World class hurdler. Our two hopefuls McCorquadale and McDonald Bailey made the final and were 5th and 6th respectively. John Parlett excelled himself with a time of 1:50 to qualify for the 800m final while the US produced yet another world class hurdler in Ray Cochran to take the 400m hurdle title in 51.1, a new record.

Monday brought Fanny Blankers-Koen the first of her four wins as she took the 100m for Holland. Mal Whitfield retained the US grip on the 800m by holding off Arthur Wint in a close finish and the day ended with Emil Zatopek just failing to catch Gaston Reiff of Belgium in monsoon-like conditions in the 5,000m, after appearing well beaten.

On Wednesday the stream of excellent performances continued with Blankers-Koen beating our own Maureen Gardner narrowly in the 80m hurdles for her second gold medal. Finland had their expected win in the men's Javelin and the USA made a clean sweep in the 110m hurdles, Bill Porter winning in 13.9.

The strength of Swedish steeplechasing was shown on the Thursday, with the first three home led by Sjoestrand in 9.04. This was followed by a memorable 400m final in which Herb McKenley was overtaken in the straight by his fellow Jamaican Arthur Wint, the 800m silver medallist.

Friday, and after another downpour yet another favourite, the World 1,500m record holder Lennart Strand was held off by his fellow Swede Henry Eriksson; our own Bill Nankeville finished a meritorious 6th in 3.52. The other final that day saw Blankers-Koen win her third gold in the 200m from Britain's Audrey Williamson.

The last day provided the expected relay wins in the men's events by the United States, the longer relay somewhat luckily after Arthur Wint pulled a muscle on the third stage while making inroads into the American lead. The women's sprint relay went to Holland, giving Fanny Blankers-Koen gold medal number four, and the Decathlon showed the world the new American discovery Bob Mathias, who at the tender age of 17 upstaged his more experienced rivals. Both walks went to Sweden but only after much dispute amongst the judges which cast a cloud over future track walks. The grand finale, the Marathon, provided its usual high drama with Cabrera of Argentina catching Belgium's Etienne Gailly four hundred metres from the tape closely, followed by Britain's Tommy Richards, who had run a very sensible race.

Belgrave Olympians

Belgrave's involvement in these stirring events were a fine 5th place in the 10,000m track walk by Harry Churcher, Bill Nankeville's equally good 6th place in the 1,500m final and Bill Lucas' run in the 5,000m heats where he was unfortunate to draw Zatopek's heat. A word should also be said about the marathon runner Etienne Gailly, for while in England in the Army, he had run for Belgrave. The runners were not Belgrave's only contribution, as a scrutiny of the programmes exhibited a number of Belgrave officials among the judges, announcers and officials who had made the Games such a success.

Team performances by the Bels during the year were first rate. Major titles over the Country included the Surrey, Southern and National titles, coupled with the South of Thames Senior and the principal road relay of the year, the London to Brighton. The walkers maintained their usual high standard by winning the National 10 mile Championship and also took the Surrey title. In the remainder of the walking Championships they were only thwarted by the excellent Sheffield and Surrey teams.

On the track, excluding those already mentioned in the Games, a number of excellent performances were produced. Alan Sexton ran a classic race to win the AAA Junior 220yd title and evergreen Charlie Smart, home on leave from Germany, finished 5th in the AAA 6 mile Championships, only a few yards away from Olympic selection. On studying the results of the closed Belgrave events and Championships one is stuck by the depth in all sections of the club and the support given to club handicaps and Championships, and the keen competition for places in Belgrave teams.

Arthur Bruce

Len Herbert and Bill Lucas were often involved in battle royal. Len, who gained his international vest in 1946, invariably used to sit in on the taller, longer striding Bill, waiting to turn on his powerful sprint in the final stretch. But on this occasion, believed to be at Wimbledon Stadium in 1951, Bill held the sprinter at bay. W.E. "Bill "Lucas, DFC, made his international debut in the heats of the 1948 Olympic 5,000m.

Photo: Ed. Lacey

items.heading: THE YACHT HANDICAP, WIMBLEDON, 3 OCT
items.summary: ARM's account of the 1992 'Yacht' Handicap at Wimbledon, won by 17-year-old Stuart Booth, with new Belgravian Kaessa Tadesse running 14:36 from an 11:15 handicap for third on the all-time list, and the full handicap result.
items.text:
THE YACHT HANDICAP, WIMBLEDON, 3 OCT

A steady drizzle did little to dampen the spirits of young Stuart Booth who must have thought it was his birthday when he found the handicapper ushering him towards the front of the indian file making up the start of the 1992 'Yacht' Handicap. But this was not the only talking point among the bystanders: a new Belgravian, Junior World Half-marathon Champion Kaessa Tadesse, an Ethiopian now settling in the UK, was making his Belgrave debut, and the field contained four ladies out to settle a few scores with male colleagues. By the time the front marker was away the field was up to 21, disappointingly four down on the previous race.

Pat Mead set off as "rabbit", a little cast down to find that Charlie Manning was a non-starter after she had voiced a pointed, "I'll see you in the 'Yacht 3'," after a recent training clash. Dennis Jones was next away and then came a short wait until a gaggle around the six-minute mark were sent off, Stuart among them and grinning like the Cheshire Cat as he rounded the turn at the end of Lauriston Road. On they came: the veterans, the faster ladies, the younger men, until Marco and Marcello brought up what would normally have been the back of the field, penalised by well over 10 minutes. As "March" disappeared along South Side and headed for the Memorial we waited ... and waited ... until at last Kaessa, suffering from an 11 minute 15 second handicap, came by looking every inch a champion. "Surely no-one can give away that much in a three mile race," says your reporter. "Don't you believe it old son," replies Mr. Carter, "but watch out, he don't know the way!" as Kaessa attempted to turn left and head for Raynes Park.

The wait. Rain dripping from trees crept under collars and into shoes and the recorder's ball-point pen gave up the ghost as speculation continued: "Wonder if Stuart's got time to stop and take a rest ... Hope Kaessa sees Marcello turn onto Windmill Road - otherwise he'll end up in Putney."

"They're at the village," went up the cry, and yes, it was Stuart Booth, well clear to take the race by no less than 1 minute and 9 seconds. But while Handicapper "Boofer" Bruce may have slipped up with the winner, his assessment of the majority of the field proved to be first rate as the front markers, although still to the fore along West Side, were being eaten up by the pack. Jim Slough and Chris Taplin were fairly comfortably 2nd and 3rd Belgravians but then came a frenzy of activity with a dozen or more all on the finishing path at the same time and Kaessa striking through the lot of them like a knife.

What a run! His 14:36 took him straight up to third spot on the all-time top 20 list behind Gerry North's epic 14:15 in 1962 and Ollie Foote's 14:34 from 1984 - and he's just 17 years old!

ARM

With many of last year's regular team members missing through injury, work, or study commitments, Belgrave turned up with rather a weak team and could only finish 8th, our lowest placing in the Surrey league since we were relegated from division one four years ago.

The press made much of the participation of two guest runners; Joseph Njugana, a Kenyan brought to the race by John Bicourt, ran without a number and won with ease and Dave Taylor, a Blackheath athlete, came an unofficial 4th.

Three laps of the undulating Brockwell Park course is a good test of Autumn fitness especially after the heavy rain we have had this season, and in spite of the lowly team performance there were some encouraging Belgrave performances.

Jim Estall ran his usual steady, reliable race and James Ryle, in his first Cross Country season for the club, did well to finish in the top fifty after perhaps a rather ambitious start. Roger Alsop, fresh from a very good track season, ran intelligently, starting cautiously and moving through the field to 55th using his speed on the downhill sections to good effect. Marcello Bizio and Brandon Reid both stuck gamely to the task although neither was 100% fit.

This year's Great North run incorporated the inaugural IAAF World Half Marathon Championships. Belgrave's Olympic 10,000m representative Paul Evans, ran another splendid race to finish 11th in 61:38 - second Briton home behind Rossendale's Dave Lewis, 7th. items.text:
SOUTH OF THAMES JUN. CC CHAMPS., MARGATE, 14 NOV

Mark Anderson reports:-

Only seven club members made the trip to Margate for this event which was held over a flat, windy and rather tedious three lap course. All those who did compete, however, performed very well and the club was rewarded with 3rd place in the 4-man team event.

Belgrave vests featured prominently at the head of the field from the start with three members amongst the leading 15 after the first mile. Roger Alsop went hard from the gun and was looking very determined as he clung to the leaders. Jim Estall was having another solid run just a few places behind Roger with James Ryle starting to move through after a cautious start.

The leading two runners moved away from the rest of the field towards the end of the first circuit with a prolonged increase in pace and Roger's valiant effort was beginning to tell on him as he began to drop back on the second lap. Meanwhile, James was looking very strong as he continued his steady progress through the field and by the start of the last lap James was right behind Jim as they both worked to combat a competitive bunch vying for fifth place.

In an exciting sprint finish Jim finished in 8th place with James 10th, but their placings could so easily have been two or three higher. Roger hung on well for 21st, holding off Mike Webb who had moved through to 27th to round off a solid team performance.

items.summary: ARM's report of the club 7.5 mile cross country championship for the "Blackstaffe" Shield on Wimbledon Common, won by Kaessa Tadesse for his first club title, with Lionel Mann's quip and Marcello Bizio winning the handicap.
items.text:
CLUB 7.5m CC CHAMPS., WIMBLEDON COMMON, 28 NOV

The dozen Belgravians involved in the Club Championship race for the "Blackstaffe" Shield took their places at the start line among many other runners taking part in the inter-club match to be held in conjunction but there was only ever going to be one winner of both events - Kaessa Tadesse. The young African was content to share the lead with the opposition for the first circuit, 14:03, but struck out on his own with a second of 14:08 and finished with a 13:51 to take the race by 15 seconds and with it his first club title.

Our royal chef Lionel Mann was back on the Common although still limping badly from the very nasty knee injury that struck him while on a walking holiday last summer. With Belgrave lying in last place in the league after the first two races Colin Pearson and other members of the committee had tried their best to persuade our middle distance stars to support the club in this important fixture. items.text:
CLUB 10m CC CHAMPS., WIMBLEDON COMMON, 23 JAN

When shortly before the race Frank Ward was seen donning a pair of shoes bearing more than a trace of damp mud, it didn't really need a Sherlock Holmes to deduce that he had been hard at work on the hills of Streatham Common during the week. Was he, therefore, returning to race fitness once more? Marcello Bizio, on the other hand, was muttering about treating the event as a training run and that he didn't need a number. A suddenly officious Gordon Biscoe was all for disqualifying him there and then but had to give way when Colin Pearson announced that he had left the numbers in his car anyway and that half the field were going to have to run without one. Still, with a field of only ten, identification was not going to be a problem.

Owain Lewes was looking pretty sharp and keeping quiet during all this preamble and sure enough, after two and a half miles it was his mud-streaked figure that led the field and held a clear advantage over Frank and Marcello. But unusually for this race, the order was to change at the front. Marcello took over to plough through the mud in his forceful style, Frank came out half-way through, evidently still some way from his best form, while Owain held up well to take the silver medal and romp away with the handicap result. Steve Willimont is turning into a most reliable engine-room man, turning out in successive weeks and fully deserving his "-bronze".

items.heading: SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR CC CHAMPS., COULSDON, 30 JAN
items.summary: Belgrave were 6th team in the South of Thames senior cross country championships on Farthing Downs, Coulsdon, with James Ryle 11th just ahead of Frank Ward.
items.text:
SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR CC CHAMPS., COULSDON, 30 JAN

This was a far more heartening performance from the cross country team on Farthing Downs, both in terms of performance and turn out. It was a credit to Colin Pearson that he managed to get not only the twelve team members, but two travelling reserves, Trevor Williams and Tony Stone, as well. Although just missing out on the medals it is worth noting that the scoring six had less points than the previous year when we were third. It was newcomer James Ryle who again produced the best run of the day finishing in 11th position, just ahead of Frank Ward. Nice to see Frank gradually returning to fitness in time for the twelve stage.

After much recent rain it was perhaps surprising to see the course fairly firm under foot apart from the muddy fields along the top of Happy Valley at the far end of the course. Two extended laps of three and a half miles with the very sharp chalky hill always proves a good test, although there are some nice flat bits as well.

Belgrave got off to a good start up the long hill with Marcello Bizio in the top eight, and Frank Ward, James Ryle and Owain Lewes all in the leading twenty. At that stage the team were looking good for medals with Roger Alsop and Mike Webb packing well in the top forty. As the race progressed James managed to get up to the back of a bunch of about four which included Frank in the top dozen as they raced along the bottom of Happy Valley.

Unfortunately for the team both Marcello and Owain began to slip back by the end of the first lap, Marcello suffering from stomach cramps which eventually saw him drop out of the race; with him went any chance of medals. Owain was suffering from an over ambitious start and the Club '10' the week before.

James and Frank had a right ding dong battle for the remainder of the race, first one ahead and then the other until eventually, with a very strong finish, James just got the better of our Treasurer - 11th to 12th. Mike Webb finished well too, just ahead of Roger Alsop who ran a steady race to close in 35th. It was a good day for the Arthur Bruce squad who provided four runners out of the leading six and Trevor Williams, running as a guest, who had his best race for some time.

SOUTH of ENGLAND CC CHAMPS., MOTE PARK, MAIDSTONE, 16 JAN

Picturesque rolling countryside, some testing inclines and a fairly stiff wind combined to make this an interesting event. Added to these elements was the uncertainty for many competitors as to whether they would even make the start line. Diversions and lengthy tailbacks heading into Maidstone resulted in many frustrated runners either still fumbling with their numbers, or launching impressive sprints towards the start line as the gun went.

Most of Belgrave's top runners stayed away from the event and after one circuit of the parkland it looked as if Marcello Bizio and Marco Mazzotta wished they had as well. Marcello, having had a miserable start to the afternoon after being held up in the traffic and failing to get Kaessa Tadesse to the start line in time for the Junior event was seen walking disconsolately away from the course while Marco also came out, visibly in pain with his back trouble having flared up again. Three runners almost immediately broke away from the field - two from H/W and our own Marcello Bizio. items.heading: READING HALF-MARATHON, 28 MAR
items.summary: Paul Evans won the Reading Half-Marathon in 1:01:38, over two minutes clear, breaking the course record by 29 seconds.
items.text:
READING HALF-MARATHON, 28 MAR

With three weeks to the London Marathon, Paul Evans blasted a spectacular warning to his rivals when he visited the Berkshire town of Reading. It might have only been a "half-marathon" but this man never does things by halves. The field included several Russians and Kenyans plus some of Britain's best road runners yet the Belgravian came home over two minutes clear in 1:01:38, a time exactly equalling his Great North Run clocking. A brutal third mile of 4:39 put paid to the hopes of the majority in the lead pack but this paled into insignificance when Paul let rip with an astounding 13:37 three miles from the six to eight mile markers! Now well clear he continued pouring on the effort and ended up smashing the six year-old course record by 29 seconds.

Just take a look at these mile timings: 4:52, 4:44, 4:39, 4:51, 4:48, 4:36, 4:30, 4:31, 4:41, 4:48, 4:32, 4:39, 4:45.

1, P.Evans (Belgrave) 1:01:38; 2, P.Whitehead (Skyrac) 1:03:32; 3, J.Kiptum (Kenya) 1:03:46.

items.text:
THAMES VALLEY H 5x3.5m ROAD RELAY, CRANFORD, 27 MAR

Best Belgrave performance on the cool, clear afternoon was the 16:46 first leg run by Roger Alsop. Roger has been training hard over the winter and looks to be coming up to peak condition for the track this Summer. After a rather cautious start, he moved steadily through the field and looked comfortable at the end.

Marcello Bizio ran 17:07 for the second leg and was followed by Daryll Maynard with 17:27. The team finished in 20th position.

items.heading: Bels raise their game for Southern Road Relay
items.summary: Report of the South of England 12-stage road relay at Thurrock, where a depleted Belgrave team managed by Colin Pearson finished 11th (10th after Hounslow's disqualification) to qualify for the National Road Relay.
items.text:
Bels raise their game for Southern Road Relay

SOUTH OF ENGLAND 12-STAGE ROAD RELAY, THURROCK, 4 APR

Perhaps 11th position may not seem much after the glories and past triumphs in the old London to Brighton and then the Belgrave 12-Stage, but this was a magnificent performance by a team decimated by illness, injuries and withdrawals.

It is a tribute to team manager Colin Pearson that he managed not only to put together a team, but one which finished high enough to qualify for the National Road Relay and in doing so beat all our rivals from the Surrey League except Boxhill, who won, and Hounslow, who only came by us after Marco Mazzotta went off course.

Throughout the afternoon, Colin's cheerful confidence spread throughout the team, half of whom were unfit, or in the case of Marcello Bizio, actually ill. He had got out of his sick bed to run. We were without Evans, Staines, Foote and Paton but it didn't matter. There was John Gladwin running in the same team as his old friend Mark Sinclair for the first time in years, the pair of them enjoying themselves and the occasion. And several others were given the chance to represent Belgrave and they ran above themselves for their club.

Of course the occasion was not like Wimbledon. The relay has been moved from our home patch because of ever increasing problems with the traffic: here the changeover was just in front of the main stand of a small running track set in the heart of a bleak part of Essex.

After the gun it was half a lap of the track, then out through a housing estate and past a handful of spectators, down a narrow, straight, flat country lane and off into the distance. Five minutes later the crocodile of runners could just be seen as they ran up the incline of the bridge over the busy Southend road. Yes, it was Giovanni Rizzo ahead, silhouetted against the electric pylons and A13 traffic a mile away. Then, not a sight of them until they returned to negotiate a nasty cross road threequarters of a mile from the finish, one which later in the day had short and long stage runners coming and going in three directions, tempers fraying, motorists honking, marshals becoming frantic - a scene all so familiar. Thurrock were learning what putting on a road relay was all about.

Boxhill led at the end of the first stage, a position they were never to lose, with Belgrave's Roger Alsop, running so well at the moment, just on 25 minutes in 24th place. Owain Lewes, who is aiming for a season of shorter track races, showed the benefit of recent speed work with one of his best runs for the club on the next short stage.

On leg three, Jim Estall produced his usual reliable run in spite of high mileage marathon training: "Can't I run two legs ?" Then a half fit Frank Ward got round on memory to hand over to Steve Halliday, down from Halifax for the race, as cheery as ever and having a blinding run with 4th fastest long stage of the day to move Belgrave up from 17th to 10th.

Progression continued with John Gladwin, again only half fit, on the next short stage, and handing on to Kaessa Tadesse who had the difficult task of setting out just behind a bunch containing Andy Bristow and Dominic Bannister, the Southern champion. Bristow ran a time second only to Eammon Martin's fastest of the day but Kaessa also ran an excellent leg and broke Bannister 1.5 miles from the finish.

Mark Sinclair ran even faster than John Gladwin, passing on to Mike Webb, rather happier on the country but as reliable as ever. Then a buoyant Darrell Maynard was a second faster than Mark. Poor Marco Mazzotta, not really fit enough for a long stage, but willing to fill in for Marcello who had been ill all week with a tooth abscess and 'flu. Marco took a wrong turning, lost at least a minute, and then ran himself to exhaustion trying to make up for it.

This left Marcello on the last leg, could he maintain 11th position and qualify the team for Sutton Park later in the month. Of course the answer was yes. When ever did Marcello let the team down in a situation like this. He ran with fire in his eyes and produced the team's fastest short stage, just ducking under 14 minutes.

In the end there was just over a minute between the leading three teams but the chasers never really got close to Boxhill who seemed to be about the only team at full strength. No, it didn't have the same atmosphere as Wimbledon, let alone the London to Brighton, but it was an enjoyable and successful day for Belgrave nevertheless.

1, Boxhill 3:47:37; 2, Southampton 3:48:14; 3, London Irish 3:48:57; ... 11, Belgrave (R.Alsop 25:00, O.Lewes 14:29, J.Estall 24:51, F.Ward 14:21, S.Halliday 23:39, J.Gladwin 14:12, K.Tadesse 24:04, M.Sinclair 14:04, M.Webb 26:35, D.Maynard 14:03, M.Mazzotta 27:56, M.Bizio 13:59) 3:57:13; 57 teams finished.

Stop press: Hounslow disqualified from Southern Road Relay - Bels. up to 10th. Colin Pearson says "They can get away with ringers in the Surrey League but not in the Southern".

items.heading: THE LONDON MARATHON, 18 APR
items.summary: Account of the 1993 London Marathon seen from Tower Bridge, where favourite Paul Evans, suffering from a sore throat, dropped out; Jim Estall was 89th and E. Martin of Basildon won.
items.text:
THE LONDON MARATHON, 18 APR

After Paul Evans' exciting 1992 season which included, of course, his fine 5th place in last year's 'London', he was most people's favourite to sweep up the honours in this year's edition of the classic. He had raced sparingly in the run-up to the event yet destroyed the field when he had ventured out in his racing kit. But we know so well that there is no such thing as a certainty in athletics where a very fine line divides the super-fit from those suffering injury or illness. Unknown to us spectators, Paul had started suffering from a sore throat on the Saturday afternoon but come the morning of the race, he was still intent on competing.

At the 'House on the Bridge', a bar on the southern approach to Tower Bridge nearing the 13 mile point, a television visible from the pavement had thoughtfully been left switched on overnight; no doubt the licensee was hoping to attract the marathon crowd when he opened later in the day. At 9.30am, like moths gathered around a candle flame, athletics fans were shoulder to shoulder on the footpath outside, noses pressed against the bar window to watch the initial stages of the race. At the early mile markers Paul could be seen in the leading pack but with the women's race due along soon it was time to desert the TV and take up a place at the barriers.

Nothing matches actually being present at a big sporting occasion. We had been warmed up by the wheelchair competitors, the Liz and Lisa show had moved on past, and now, with the energy of a tide in full flood, the leaders in the men's field, a group some thirty strong, burst around the corner from Abbey Street into Tower Bridge Road with the accompanying cheering and flag waving from the watchers being pushed along ahead of them like so much flotsam.

Where was Paul? There - no that's the tall blonde Polish runner. What could have happened. Jim Estall came by and cheerfully waved back on hearing his name called. Some hundreds of runners streamed through before Evans was sighted, a mere shadow of his normal self and, to be honest, looking quite unwell. He came out somewhere over the bridge and must have been bitterly disappointed to leave the race in the hands of those he had previously been confident of beating.

Nevertheless, he has already been selected for the World Champs. in Stuttgart and if he can pop out that 2:08 effort then, without the prior warning of 'London', it's going to cause an even greater shock.

items.heading: NATIONAL 12-STAGE ROAD RELAY, SUTTON PARK, 24 APR
items.summary: Report of the National 12-stage road relay at Sutton Park, won by Shaftesbury Barnet, with an illness-hit Belgrave 35th, Steve Halliday going off course while leading the first stage.
items.text:
NATIONAL 12-STAGE ROAD RELAY, SUTTON PARK, 24 APR

It was in 1974 that the National Road Relay was held for the first time at Sutton Park and there have been some impressive runs by individuals and teams throughout the intervening years. This year the winning time was well outside the top ten but for excitement it was second to none. The Midland clubs, who hold their area championship on the same course, were strongly tipped to provide the medallists but when it came to the 'cards down' it was the South that held the aces. The Shaftesbury Barnet team manager judged things just right, for John Sherban, on the penultimate leg, set the fastest long stage time of the day in turning a 30 second deficit into a 55 second lead. And then the thrills continued with Boxhill Racers, through Tom Bignall, moving from outside the frame into 2nd spot on the very last lap while Swansea's tail-end super-vets held the chasing hordes at bay for 3rd.

The Belgrave outfit was again hit by illness and injury with young Marlon Anderson getting pretty close to the action as next on the reserve list.

Stage 1 was taken by Steve Halliday who was most certainly on for one of the fastest times of the day - except that while holding a 70 yard lead over the field he went off course, lost about a minute, and then trailed in a disconsolate 18th!

Our fastest short stage came from Roger Alsop on leg 2. He covered the 3m 8y in 14:40 to retrieve three places and, bearing in mind the gradients, set a time which must equate to about 15 minutes for 5,000m, a target he surely must achieve before too long.

Kaessa Tadesse was the pick of the rest of our long stage runners, benefiting from Steve's misfortune to become our fastest over the 5m 706y stretch with 26:06, and Johnny G took yet another step along the road to fitness by running a 14:50 effort that makes an appearance over 800m in our team for Budapest begin to look a real possibility.

1, Shaftesbury Barnet 4:06:24; 2, Boxhill Racers 4:07:01; 3, Swansea 4:07:07; ... 35, Belgrave 4:20:42.
